item.title: Your PRs Get Reviewed When Someone Has Time — Wire `anthropics/claude-code-action` to Pull Request Events and Claude Code Reviews Every Push Against Your CLAUDE.md
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: anthropics/claude-code-action runs Claude Code inside GitHub Actions. Add it to a pull_request trigger and every push gets an automated review against your project CLAUDE.md standards.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: `anthropics/claude-code-action` puts a full Claude Code session inside your GitHub Actions workflow — trigger it on `pull_request` events to get an automated review on every push, governed by your CLAUDE.md.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** configure a Claude Code review job that runs on every PR open and update, reads your CLAUDE.md standards as its brief, and posts inline comments — no human reviewer needed for the first pass.
**Setup — two paths:**
The fast path: run `/install-github-app` from Claude Code in your terminal. It installs the Claude GitHub App on your repo and walks you through adding the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret.
The manual path, if the command isn't available: 1. Install the [Claude GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/claude) on your repo. 2. Add `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as a repository secret. 3. Add a workflow file:
```yaml name: Claude PR Review on: pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize]
permissions: contents: read pull-requests: write id-token: write # required even with your own token
jobs: review: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with: anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }} prompt: "Review this PR against the project standards in CLAUDE.md. Post specific inline comments on lines that need changes." claude_args: "--allowedTools Read,Bash" ```
**CLAUDE.md does the work:** the Action runs in the same environment as a local Claude Code session, which means it reads your `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and project rules. Put your review criteria there — coding conventions, required test coverage, security rules — and the Action enforces them without a separate prompt. Code that meets your CLAUDE.md standards gets fewer comments; code that doesn't gets flagged consistently.
**Restrict tools explicitly:** without `--allowedTools`, Claude Code has write access to your repository. For a review job that only reads and comments, `--allowedTools Read,Bash` is a safe default. If you need Claude to fix things, add `Edit` — but then review what it commits.
**Limits:** Each run bills API tokens against your Anthropic account (a 500-line diff typically uses 10–30K tokens at Sonnet rates). The Action defaults to Sonnet; use the `model` parameter to upgrade for complex codebases. Review latency runs 1–3 minutes depending on PR size. For large PRs with many files, the context window fills before all files are reviewed — scope Claude's attention with a focused prompt or a per-directory CLAUDE.md.
**Sources:** [Claude Code GitHub Actions docs — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions) · [Autonomous PR review walkthrough — startdebugging.net](https://startdebugging.net/2026/05/how-to-run-claude-code-in-a-github-action-for-autonomous-pr-review/) · [Claude Code GitHub Actions CI/CD guide — wmedia.es](https://wmedia.es/en/tips/claude-code-github-actions-pr-review)

item.title: Your RAG Retriever Misses Exact Product Names and Technical Identifiers — Combine BM25 and Vector Search With `EnsembleRetriever` for the Gaps Dense Embeddings Can't Fill
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Dense embeddings encode meaning but struggle with rare tokens, product names, and exact identifiers. BM25 handles those. LangChain EnsembleRetriever merges both with Reciprocal Rank Fusion in under 10 lines.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Dense embeddings miss exact product names, error codes, and rare tokens that BM25 catches; `EnsembleRetriever` merges both retrievers via Reciprocal Rank Fusion in under 10 lines.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** add a BM25 retriever alongside your existing vector store, merge their results with weighted RRF, and get higher recall on queries that contain identifiers, model names, or technical terms your embedding model blurs together.
**Why dense alone falls short:**
Embedding models compress semantics. That's a feature for paraphrase matching — but it's a bug when the query is `"gpt-4o-mini"` and your corpus mentions `"gpt-4o-mini"` exactly. The embedding treats those as nearly identical to `"GPT-4o Mini"`, `"OpenAI mini model"`, and sometimes `"small GPT"`. BM25 uses token overlap: if the query term appears in the document, it scores it, regardless of semantic similarity.
The pattern that works: BM25 for recall on exact terms and rare tokens; dense vectors for recall on synonyms and paraphrases; RRF to merge.
**Setup:**
```bash pip install rank_bm25 langchain-community ```
```python from langchain_community.retrievers import BM25Retriever from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma from langchain.retrievers import EnsembleRetriever
# Your existing docs list bm25_retriever = BM25Retriever.from_documents(docs) bm25_retriever.k = 5
vector_store = Chroma.from_documents(docs, embedding=embeddings) vector_retriever = vector_store.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5})
ensemble = EnsembleRetriever( retrievers=[bm25_retriever, vector_retriever], weights=[0.4, 0.6] )
results = ensemble.invoke("gpt-4o-mini rate limits") ```
`EnsembleRetriever` runs both retrievers in parallel, then merges their ranked lists using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Documents that rank highly in both lists float to the top; documents that only appear in one are penalized proportionally. The `weights` parameter scales RRF scores before fusion — 0.4/0.6 biases toward semantic similarity while still giving BM25 a meaningful voice.
**Three things that break this in production:**
1. **BM25 rebuilds from scratch on update** — there's no incremental index; every new document means rebuilding the full BM25 index. At a few thousand documents this is fast (< 1 second); at a million it becomes a bottleneck. At that scale, use a vector store with native sparse support (Qdrant and Elasticsearch both offer hybrid retrieval without maintaining a separate BM25 index). 2. **Weights need tuning per domain** — the default 0.5/0.5 split works for general text; technical documentation with many exact identifiers often benefits from 0.5+ weight on BM25. 3. **Deduplication by content hash** — `EnsembleRetriever` deduplicates by document content. If your documents have different metadata but identical text, only one copy comes back. Use distinct content or handle deduplication upstream.
**Sources:** [EnsembleRetriever how-to — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/ensemble_retriever/) · [BM25Retriever integration — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/providers/rank_bm25) · [Hybrid search with BM25 and semantic search — blog.lancedb.com](https://blog.lancedb.com/hybrid-search-combining-bm25-and-semantic-search-for-better-results-with-lan-1358038fe7e6) · [How to Use Hybrid Search for Better LLM RAG Retrieval — learn.aisingapore.org](https://learn.aisingapore.org/2024/08/how-to-use-hybrid-search-for-better-llm-rag-retrieval-by-dr-leon-eversberg-aug-2024/)

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Has 200 Lines Because You've Never Run /doctor — It Flags Codebase-Derivable Content and Warns When You Cross 40 K Characters
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run /doctor in Claude Code to find CLAUDE.md bloat — it flags size warnings at 40 K characters and identifies content Claude can already derive from your committed files.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: `/doctor` audits your CLAUDE.md for size bloat and content Claude could derive from the codebase itself; v2.1.206 (July 2026) added the codebase-derivable check.**
Every line in CLAUDE.md loads on every request. Rules that document things Claude can already read from your project — the tech stack, the directory layout, that you're on Node 22 — burn context window on every conversation and can mask real conflicts. `/doctor` checks for this.
**What /doctor flags:**
``` /doctor ```
1. **CLAUDE.md size** — warns when you cross 40 K characters (community-tested threshold; not stated in official docs). Over that, every conversation starts with a heavy always-on load. 2. **Codebase-derivable content** — added in v2.1.206. If CLAUDE.md documents things visible in package.json, tsconfig, the directory tree, or other committed files, `/doctor` proposes removing them. Claude reads those files; the CLAUDE.md copy is redundant noise. 3. **Local vs. committed duplicates** — if your user CLAUDE.md (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) restates rules from the project file, it flags the overlap.
**How to trim:**
Review each proposed cut before accepting. `/doctor` can't tell whether a rule is there for a reason it couldn't discover — a one-line override for a framework default, an edge case that bit the team. When in doubt, keep it and add a brief inline note explaining why it's explicit.
Practical order: remove tech-stack documentation first (Claude reads package.json and tsconfig), then remove directory descriptions that match what an `ls` already shows. Keep anything that overrides a default, resolves an ambiguity, or records a past mistake.
**Limit:** `/doctor` reports tooling mismatches (missing Node version, broken MCP connections) but doesn't fix them — structural problems require manual repair. And the 40 K size threshold comes from community testing, not official docs; treat it as a signal, not a hard rule.
**Sources:** [Claude Code best practices — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) · [/doctor command guide 2026 — thepromptshelf.dev](https://thepromptshelf.dev/blog/claude-code-doctor-checkup-command-guide-2026/) · [v2.1.206 release notes — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20260710-cc-updates-v2-1-206/)

item.title: Your Existing Component Lives in Code and You Want to Explore a Visual Change — /design export Pushes It Into Claude Design as a Live Prototype
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Use /design export in Claude Code to push an existing component into Claude Design as a live prototype, explore visual changes in the design surface, then import the result back as code.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: `/design export` takes an existing component from your codebase into Claude Design as a live visual prototype; `/design import` brings the design changes back as code edits — the reverse of the standard handoff direction.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Take a component that already exists in your codebase, push it into Claude Design for visual exploration without touching the codebase, make layout or styling changes in the design surface, and pull those changes back as code — without rebuilding from a screenshot.
**Three things to know before you start:**
- `/design export` reads your component and creates an editable Claude Design prototype; `/design import <id>` applies design changes back as code edits in Claude Code (requires v2.1.233+, research preview on Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise) - Claude Design uses your Tailwind config, CSS tokens, and component exports as generation context, so explorations start from what your app actually renders rather than generic defaults - The bundle carries visual structure and styling; it doesn't carry runtime behavior, API calls, or state management — expect to wire those after the import
**Walk-through:**
```bash # Step 1: Export an existing component as a Claude Design prototype /design export --component src/components/CheckoutSummary.tsx
# Claude publishes a live prototype and returns the project ID # Design project created: cd_proj_abc123 # View at: https://claude.ai/design/cd_proj_abc123
# Step 2: Open the link in Claude Design (browser) # Explore layout changes, spacing adjustments, variant directions # No code changes needed during this phase — iterate freely
# Step 3: Pull design changes back into the codebase /design import cd_proj_abc123 # Claude Code reads the updated bundle and applies # visual changes as code edits to the component file ```
**What survives the return trip:** layout changes, spacing, color tokens, component hierarchy. **What doesn't:** any behavior wired up after the last export — route handlers, fetch calls, context subscriptions need re-review after the import.
**How this differs from `/design-sync`:** Sync pushes your design system (all components, tokens) into the canvas as a generation context. Export starts from one specific component in code and creates a prototype of it. Use export when you're exploring a rework of something that already exists; use sync when starting a new feature from scratch.
A hands-on test from April 2026 found that Claude Design reads your component files as design artifacts, not as an editable component graph — the generated canvas looks right but isn't directly linked to your library's internals. That gap means you should treat the round-trip as "visual diff to apply," not as a lossless sync.
**Sources:** [Get started with Claude Design — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design) · [Claude Design hands-on: what it generates and what it doesn't — ice-ice-bear.github.io](https://ice-ice-bear.github.io/posts/2026-04-22-claude-design/) · [/design skill, w34 release notes — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/whats-new/2026-w34)

item.title: The Standalone claude.ai/design Site Closes December 14 — Migrate Your Design Systems Through Artifacts Before Then or Lose Your Projects
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic's official migration guide confirms claude.ai/design shuts down December 14, 2026. Design systems migrate through Artifacts; chats, comments, and public share links are permanently deleted.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: claude.ai/design shuts down December 14, 2026; design systems migrate through the Artifacts page in Claude, but chats, comments, and public share links are permanently deleted.**
Anthropic's [official migration guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17440474-migrate-from-standalone-claude-design-to-claude) confirms the closure. After December 14 the standalone address redirects to Claude.
**What moves:**
- **Design systems** — migrate one to bring over all systems in the organization, via the Artifacts page in Claude - **Project files** — open projects carry over into Claude
**What doesn't:**
- Chats and comments in the standalone site are deleted permanently - Public share links break — anyone visiting an old `/design` share URL loses access - No export-and-reimport path for chat history
**Where to work after closure:**
The design workflow continues through two paths:
1. **Claude.ai** — design systems live alongside conversations in Artifacts; the canvas is accessible from any Claude conversation 2. **Claude Code** — the `/design` skill (research preview, v2.1.233+) lets you create, edit, import, and export designs without leaving the terminal, and connects to Claude Design via MCP
If you've used the standalone site and have design systems there, the migration window is about 38 days from today.
**Why it matters:** Public project links break permanently. If you've shared a claude.ai/design URL with a team, embedded it in documentation, or used it as a client handoff link, replace those links before December 14. Chats contain prompt history that isn't downloadable after closure — save anything you'd want to reference.

item.title: You're Using Claude Code When You Should Be in Claude Design, and Vice Versa — the Decision Rule That Ends the Guessing
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Regenerate in Claude Design when you need to explore layout or interaction; switch to Claude Code once you're modifying real components, wiring behavior, or conforming to repo rules.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Regenerate in Claude Design when you need to explore layout or interaction; switch to Claude Code once you're modifying real components, wiring behavior, or conforming to repo rules.**
After the first handoff, every component change raises the same question: go back to the design tool, or iterate in the editor? The wrong choice costs time — either generating code you then have to reconcile with your codebase, or manually implementing a visual change that would take two prompts in the design surface.
**Stay in Claude Code when:** - The change involves props, event handlers, or data shape — implementation details - The component is already in your codebase with passing tests - The fix must conform to your TypeScript types, design tokens, or component API - It's a targeted correction, not an exploration
**Go back to Claude Design when:** - The layout, information hierarchy, or interaction model needs to change - You want to compare two or three directions before writing any code - You haven't decided what it should look like — you need to see it - The current approach is structurally wrong, not just incorrectly implemented
The asymmetry matters: an April 2026 hands-on review found Claude Design doesn't modify an existing component library's real code — it generates output that resembles your components. That gap is why the handoff is non-trivial. Once Claude Code has significantly customized a component, regenerating in Claude Design produces something you'll need to reconcile.
**The round-trip cost:** `/design-sync` can push your component state back to the canvas (June 2026 two-way sync), but only published components in your team library are mappable. Changes Claude Code made directly to component internals don't surface automatically — the round-trip cost grows the further you've diverged.
Limit: This decision logic applies on the second iteration and beyond. First time through, start in Claude Design; the rule applies when you're iterating on something that already exists in the codebase.
**Sources:** [Claude Design hands-on review — ice-ice-bear.github.io](https://ice-ice-bear.github.io/posts/2026-04-22-claude-design/) · [Claude Code and Claude Design two-way sync — pasqualepillitteri.it](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/5308/claude-code-claude-design-two-way-sync-design-sync) · [Claude Design guide — studiomeyer.io](https://studiomeyer.io/en/blog/claude-design-guide)

item.title: Your MCP Server Approvals Don't Protect Against Tool Description Poisoning — Scan, Hook, and Audit Before Adding Another Server
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Tool description poisoning runs before permission prompts fire — scan tool descriptions for changes, log every MCP call with a PreToolUse hook, and prune your connected server list.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Tool description poisoning runs before permission prompts — scan descriptions for changes, log every MCP call with a PreToolUse hook, and prune the connected server list.**
A March 2026 paper from UBC ([arXiv:2603.21642](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21642)) tested seven MCP clients — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, Continue, Gemini CLI, and Langflow — for prompt injection vulnerabilities. The finding most relevant to Claude Code users: tool description poisoning is the attack that bypasses permission dialogs. Claude Code reads tool descriptions during planning, before any `always_ask` prompt fires. Instructions embedded there execute in the model's reasoning before you see anything.
**Three things worth wiring up now:**
**1. Scan and pin tool descriptions:** ```bash uvx mcp-scan@latest scan # first run: hashes each server's tool descriptions uvx mcp-scan@latest scan # subsequent runs: alerts on any change ``` A server that updates its description after you've trusted it — a rug pull — becomes visible. Limit: `mcp-scan` sends tool names and descriptions to `invariantlabs.ai`. Use `uvx mcp-scan@latest inspect` to review descriptions locally without transmitting them.
**2. Log MCP calls with a PreToolUse hook:** ```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [{ "matcher": "mcp__", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME $CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" >> ~/.claude/mcp-audit.log"}] }] } } ``` An append-only record of every MCP call, keyed to tool name and input, independent of Claude Code's own logging.
**3. Audit the connected list:** ```bash claude mcp list ``` Remove servers you're not actively using. The attack surface is exactly this list.
None of these is a complete defense — the arXiv paper found no fully immune client across all seven tested. The goal is raising the bar on unattended exploitation, not eliminating risk.
**Sources:** [Are AI-assisted Development Tools Immune to Prompt Injection? — arXiv:2603.21642](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21642) · [mcp-scan — PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-scan/) · [Claude Code hooks — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) · [Aptible MCP Security](https://aptible.com/mcp-security/mcp-prompt-injection)

item.title: Your Specialized Subagents Load 400 Lines of Project Rules They Never Use — `omitClaudeMd: true` Strips Them From Startup Context
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.271 adds omitClaudeMd: true as a frontmatter field for custom subagents — set it on narrow-task agents (schema checks, linters, file scans) to skip loading project CLAUDE.md entirely.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `omitClaudeMd: true` in a custom subagent's frontmatter and it starts without any project CLAUDE.md — useful for narrow-task agents where your project rules are irrelevant noise.**
When you fan out work to custom subagents, each one inherits your full CLAUDE.md hierarchy by default — the same 400+ lines written for the orchestrator session. A subagent whose job is to scan a schema file, run a linter, or do a targeted code search doesn't need your deployment runbook, design system conventions, or database migration policy. Unused context wastes window space and can cause the subagent to apply rules that don't belong to its task.
Claude Code v2.1.271 (September 14, 2026) added `omitClaudeMd: true` as a frontmatter field for custom subagent definitions at `.claude/agents/<name>.md`:
```markdown --- name: schema-auditor description: Checks database schema files for naming and type violations omitClaudeMd: true --- You receive a schema file path. Output a JSON array of violations... ```
With the flag set, the subagent doesn't load user, project, or local CLAUDE.md files. Organization-level managed policy files still load — the flag removes the project-specific layer, not the organization-enforced one. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files that would normally load on-demand are also skipped.
The flag also works in `--agents` JSON definitions passed to the CLI, and in plugin subagents.
**When to use it:** Narrow-task subagents with a fixed input/output contract — file analysis, schema validation, search, test runners, linters. Any subagent that only needs to know *its own instructions*, not the broader project context.
**When not to use it:** Orchestrator agents, any subagent that edits code in the repo, or anything that needs to follow project-wide conventions. Keep it off unless you have a reason to strip context.
**Limit:** `omitClaudeMd` only applies to custom subagents defined in `.claude/agents/` or via `--agents` JSON. It has no effect on built-in subagents (Explore, Plan) — those follow their own context rules.
**Sources:** [Claude Code memory docs — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) · [v2.1.271 changelog summary — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20260915-cc-updates-v2-1-272/) · [omitClaudeMd explained — claudelog.com](https://claudelog.com/faqs/what-is-omit-claude-md-in-claude-code/)

item.title: Your OpenAI SDK Already Has a Faster Path to 70B+ Models — Two Lines Route It to Fireworks AI's Inference Endpoint
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Point your OpenAI SDK at https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1 with a Fireworks API key and access a catalog of 70B+ hosted models using the same code you already have. Function calling works; streaming + tools does not.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Change `base_url` to `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1`, swap in a Fireworks model ID, and your existing OpenAI SDK code hits Fireworks' hosted inference fleet — no other changes required.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Call a 70B+ instruction-tuned model for structured output or function calling through the same OpenAI SDK your app already uses, without managing GPU infrastructure or working around per-minute rate limits.
Fireworks AI runs a hosted inference fleet optimized for throughput on large open-weight models. Its API is fully OpenAI-compatible.
**Three things to know before you start:** - Model IDs use a path format: `accounts/fireworks/models/<name>` — e.g., `accounts/fireworks/models/llama-v3p1-70b-instruct` - Function calling works; streaming is not currently supported for tool-call responses — set `stream=False` on any tool-use path - The native `fireworks-ai` Python SDK is still in alpha; the OpenAI SDK route below is the stable path
**Setup:**
```bash pip install openai export FIREWORKS_API_KEY="your_api_key_here" ```
**First call:**
```python import os from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( base_url="https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1", api_key=os.environ["FIREWORKS_API_KEY"], )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="accounts/fireworks/models/llama-v3p1-70b-instruct", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this in one sentence: ..."}], max_tokens=200, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
**Function calling:**
Replace the model with one from [Fireworks' function-calling catalog](https://docs.fireworks.ai/models/overview). Pass tools the same way you would with OpenAI. Check `response.choices[0].finish_reason == "tool_calls"` to detect when the model requests a function. Do not set `stream=True` on tool-use requests — it is not yet supported.
**Where Fireworks wins:** High-throughput workloads on 70B+ models where you need sub-second time-to-first-token and structured output. Where it's not the best fit: at 7B–13B scale, Together AI and OpenRouter (covered in [this earlier post](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-22-01-together-ai-openai-sdk-base-url-open-models)) often have lower latency; Fireworks' pricing advantage is most visible at larger model sizes.
**Limits:** Model names and availability change frequently — always check the [model catalog](https://docs.fireworks.ai/models/overview) rather than hardcoding a name. The native SDK is alpha and may break across minor versions. No streaming support for function calling means you need a different code path if you're streaming and calling tools.
**Sources:** [Fireworks quickstart — docs.fireworks.ai](https://docs.fireworks.ai/getting-started/quickstart) · [LlamaIndex Fireworks function-calling cookbook — developers.llamaindex.ai](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework/integrations/llm/fireworks_cookbook/) · [Together vs OpenRouter vs Fireworks comparison (earlier in this series)](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-22-01-together-ai-openai-sdk-base-url-open-models)

item.title: Claude Code Edits .env on Every Run Until You Add a 12-Line PreToolUse Hook
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A PreToolUse hook that exits 2 on a file-match blocks any Edit or Write call before it runs — .env, production configs, and secret files become write-locked for the whole session.
item.content:encoded:
**A PreToolUse hook that exits 2 on a file-match blocks any Edit or Write call before it runs — `.env`, production configs, and secret files become write-locked for the whole session.**
Claude Code's hook system fires scripts at four points in the tool lifecycle. PostToolUse hooks run after a tool succeeds; they can't stop it. PreToolUse hooks fire before the tool runs and can block it: exit code 2 blocks the call and shows Claude the hook's stderr; exit code 0 allows it; exit code 1 adds a warning but still allows.
**Write `.claude/hooks/protect-files.sh`:**
```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Blocks Edit/Write to any file matching the blocklist. BLOCKLIST=(".env" ".env.*" "*.pem" "private-key.*" "production.yml" "secrets.*") FILE=$(echo "$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT" | jq -r '.file_path // .path // empty') [ -z "$FILE" ] && exit 0 BASE=$(basename "$FILE") for PATTERN in "${BLOCKLIST[@]}"; do if [[ "$BASE" == $PATTERN ]]; then echo "BLOCKED: $FILE is in the write-protected list" >&2 exit 2 fi done exit 0 ```
**Wire it in `.claude/settings.json`:**
```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/protect-files.sh" }] } ] } } ```
Claude Code passes the tool's input JSON in `CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT`; `jq` extracts the target path. The exit 2 sends Claude the stderr message so it knows why it was blocked — without it, Claude retries and fails again silently.
**Two limits to know:** First, this hook fires on every Edit and Write call, so keep the check fast (a `jq` parse is milliseconds). Second, the hook doesn't fire on `Bash` calls that write files directly — pair it with a Bash pre-hook or allowlist to close that gap. Secret scan hooks (which block `git commit/push` when secrets appear in the diff) are complementary, not a replacement, for this guard.
**How it fits the hooks series:** PostToolUse handles what happens after a tool succeeds; Stop hooks gate when Claude ends a turn; PreToolUse is the place to intercept before damage is done. All three can coexist.

item.title: Claude Code Builds a New Button Component Every Time Because Figma's MCP Server Doesn't Know Your Button Exists — Code Connect Maps It in Three Steps
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Figma Code Connect links library components to their real source files; the MCP server then tells Claude Code exactly which import and props to use instead of generating a duplicate.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Configure Figma Code Connect so Claude Code reads a Figma frame via the MCP server and generates code that uses your existing components — not new duplicates with the wrong props.
**Three things to know first:** - Figma Code Connect links a Figma component to its real source file by writing a `.figma.ts` mapping file alongside your component; the Figma MCP server reads those mappings and passes them to Claude Code as context when you paste a Figma URL - Without Code Connect, Claude Code sees a visual design and guesses — it generates a component that looks right but uses the wrong props, naming, or file structure - Code Connect only works with components published to a Figma team library; unpublished components are invisible to the mapping
**Step 1 — Install the Figma MCP server and authenticate:**
```bash claude mcp add --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp ```
Open a new Claude Code session, run `/mcp`, and authenticate in the browser. Confirm with `/mcp status figma`.
Alternatively, install the bundled plugin (which also adds Code Connect skills): ```bash claude plugin install figma@claude-plugins-official ```
**Step 2 — Write a Code Connect mapping for one component:**
Create `src/components/Button.figma.ts` alongside your existing `Button.tsx`:
```typescript import figma from '@figma/code-connect' import { Button } from './Button'
figma.connect(Button, 'https://www.figma.com/file/ABC123/Design-System?node-id=1-2', { props: { variant: figma.enum('Variant', { primary: 'primary', secondary: 'secondary', ghost: 'ghost', }), disabled: figma.boolean('Disabled'), label: figma.string('Label'), }, example: ({ variant, disabled, label }) => ( <Button variant={variant} disabled={disabled}>{label}</Button> ), }) ```
The `node-id` comes from the Figma URL when you select the library component. Set `FIGMA_ACCESS_TOKEN` in your env, then push the mapping:
```bash npx figma connect publish ```
Start with 5–10 high-use primitives (Button, Input, Card, Badge). Connecting every component upfront is impractical and unnecessary.
**Step 3 — Test the loop:**
Paste a Figma frame URL into Claude Code:
``` Implement this screen using our existing components: https://www.figma.com/file/ABC123/Design-System?node-id=5-10 ```
With Code Connect configured, the generated output will say `import { Button } from './components/Button'` and use `variant="primary"` — your actual API — instead of inventing `<button className="bg-blue-500 rounded px-4">`.
**What it doesn't do:** Code Connect maps component usage, not layout logic. Claude still decides how to assemble components in a grid, handle responsive breakpoints, and what to do with unmapped components. Plan to audit the first few generations and add mappings for your most-used components before running at scale.
**One real limit:** A stale mapping — Figma component updated, mapping not republished — is worse than no mapping. Claude Code receives the old props as authoritative and generates confidently wrong code. Build `npx figma connect publish` into your design-system update process, not a one-time setup step.
**Sources:** [Figma Code Connect — Figma Developers](https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/skill-figma-code-connect) · [Claude Code and Figma: Set up the MCP server — Figma Help](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/39888612464151-Claude-Code-and-Figma-Set-up-the-MCP-server) · [Figma MCP server guide — GitHub](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide) · [Figma to Claude Code workflow — superdesign.dev](https://superdesign.dev/blog/figma-to-claude-code)

item.title: Your Agent Runs Three Tool Calls Sequentially When They Could All Go in One Turn — One System Prompt Sentence Drops Latency to the Longest Single Call
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add "issue independent tool calls together in one response turn" to your system prompt and wall-clock latency drops from sum(T_i) to max(T_i) — no other code changes needed.
item.content:encoded:
**When tool calls are independent, one sentence in your system prompt batches them into a single turn — wall-clock latency drops from the sum of each call to the longest one.**
Your agent fetches an account balance, today's exchange rate, and a user record in three sequential turns because Claude doesn't know they're independent. The pattern: Claude calls tool → you return a result → Claude calls the next tool. Three round-trips instead of one.
**The fix — add this to your system prompt:**
``` When multiple tool calls are independent (no data dependency between them), issue them all in a single response turn as separate tool_use blocks. ```
Claude Code's own system prompt includes this instruction — that's why it batches file reads and directory listings in one turn. Add it to your own agent loops and Claude will start grouping independent reads.
**Why it matters:**
For N independent calls with latencies T₁, T₂, T₃: - **Without batching:** T₁ + T₂ + T₃ + (round-trip overhead × 3) - **With batching:** max(T₁, T₂, T₃) + (round-trip overhead × 1)
Three 300 ms tool calls: ~1.0 s → ~0.4 s per batch. Longer-running tools — database queries, external APIs — make this more dramatic.
**When not to batch:** Tools with side effects or data dependencies must stay sequential — `create_account` then `fetch_account` is not safe to batch. Make dependencies explicit in your tool descriptions so Claude can reason about which calls can't be grouped. A description like "Returns the account created in the previous step" tells Claude those two calls are ordered.
**One limit to check first:** Some agent SDKs and frameworks run a serial loop over `response.content` regardless of whether Claude issued multiple `tool_use` blocks in one turn. If your harness dispatches tools sequentially by design, the batching instruction shifts only where the latency sits — not how much there is. Verify your harness actually dispatches in parallel; see the [companion post on handling multiple tool_use blocks](/ai-news/2026-09-26-02-claude-parallel-tool-calls) for the execution-side code (asyncio.gather / Promise.all).
**Sources:** [Anthropic tool use guide](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use) · [Claude Code system prompt, community gist (Jan 2026)](https://gist.github.com/chigkim/1f37bb2be98d97c952fd79cbb3efb1c6)

item.title: Every Agent Loop Re-Encodes Your System Prompt Even When Nothing Changed — Add One `cache_control` Field and Skip That Cost on Every Subsequent Call
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"} to your system prompt content block; the API caches that prefix and subsequent calls that reuse it bill at roughly 10% of full input token price, per Anthropic's pricing docs.
item.content:encoded:
**Add `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` to your system prompt content block; calls that hit the cache bill at roughly 10% of full input token price, per Anthropic's pricing documentation — but cache writes cost 125% of base input tokens, so the break-even is around two reuses.**
If your agent runs many turns against the same system prompt — a tool list, a retrieved knowledge base, a large set of coding standards — you pay full input-token rates to re-encode that content on every single call. Prompt caching marks a prefix to be stored server-side so subsequent calls within the TTL window skip the encode.
**Add a cache breakpoint:**
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, system=[ { "type": "text", "text": "You are an expert code reviewer...
[500+ lines of standards and examples]", "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"} # mark the prefix to cache } ], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review this PR diff: ..."}] ) ```
The API caches everything up to and including that block. Calls within the TTL that share the same prefix up to that point are cache hits.
**Extend to 1 hour:**
```python "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"} ```
The default TTL is 5 minutes. Use `"1h"` for agent loops or batch jobs with gaps between calls longer than 5 minutes.
**Where it matters most:** long system prompts (tool catalogs, full coding standards, documents you prepend to every call), agent loops with many turns against the same context, batch jobs running the same system prompt across hundreds of inputs.
**Real limits — these determine whether caching helps you at all:**
- **Cache writes cost 125% of base input tokens, per Anthropic's pricing docs.** A prompt you use once or change every call costs *more* with caching enabled. Break-even is roughly two cache reads per write. - **Up to 4 `cache_control` breakpoints per request.** If you mark more, the system tracks the last 4; earlier ones go uncached. - **Minimum cacheable prefix varies by model** (per Anthropic's docs: 2,048 tokens for Sonnet and Opus, 1,024 for Haiku). Prefixes shorter than the minimum are accepted but not cached. - **Tool definitions count toward the cached prefix.** If your tool list changes between calls, the cache misses — even if the system prompt text is identical. - **The cache is per-API-key.** A second key with the same system prompt starts a cold cache.
The practical test: if your system prompt is long enough to exceed the minimum and you reuse it across multiple turns in a session, caching pays. A single-turn script with a short system prompt does not benefit.
**Sources:** [Prompt caching — Anthropic docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Cache breakpoint glossary — PromptLayer](https://www.promptlayer.com/glossary/cache-breakpoint) · [Anthropic prompt caching via proxy — Orq.ai](https://docs.orq.ai/docs/proxy/providers/anthropic/prompt-caching)

item.title: Your Retriever Returns Every Document When You Asked for the High-Rated Ones — LangChain's SelfQueryRetriever Parses Structured Filters Out of Plain English Before the Vector Search Runs
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: SelfQueryRetriever calls an LLM to parse structured constraints from your query and passes them as a metadata pre-filter alongside the vector search — so "sci-fi films from 2020 rated above 8" becomes year>=2020, genre=sci-fi, rating>8 before retrieval.
item.content:encoded:
**LangChain's `SelfQueryRetriever` calls an LLM to extract structured filters from your query string and passes them to the vector store as a pre-filter — "sci-fi films from 2020 rated above 8" automatically becomes a year>=2020, genre=sci-fi, rating>8 filter run alongside the semantic search.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Write natural-language queries that automatically filter by year, author, source, or any metadata field stored with your chunks - Avoid post-filtering (which can return fewer than k results) by pushing the filter into the vector store before retrieval - Handle queries that mix semantic content with structured constraints without custom parsing code
The official how-to is at [python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/self_query](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/self_query); the Chroma-specific walkthrough at [python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/retrievers/self_query/chroma_self_query](https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/retrievers/self_query/chroma_self_query) is runnable in a notebook.
**Setup:**
```bash pip install langchain langchain-chroma langchain-anthropic lark ```
The `lark` package is required to parse the LLM-generated filter expressions. The retriever raises a clear error if it is missing.
**Build the retriever:**
```python from langchain_chroma import Chroma from langchain.retrievers.self_query.base import SelfQueryRetriever from langchain.chains.query_constructor.schema import AttributeInfo from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
# Documents must carry metadata when you embed them: # Document(page_content="...", metadata={"genre": "sci-fi", "year": 2020, "rating": 8.3})
vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(docs, embedding)
metadata_field_info = [ AttributeInfo(name="genre", description="Movie genre", type="string"), AttributeInfo(name="year", description="Release year as an integer", type="integer"), AttributeInfo(name="rating", description="IMDB rating 1-10", type="float"), ]
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-5-5", temperature=0) retriever = SelfQueryRetriever.from_llm( llm, vectorstore, "Movie summaries and ratings", metadata_field_info, ) ```
**Query in plain English:**
```python # The retriever calls the LLM once to generate: # filter={year: {$gte: 2020}, genre: {$eq: "sci-fi"}, rating: {$gt: 8}} # query="sci-fi films" # Then runs both the filter and similarity search in one vector store call. docs = retriever.invoke("sci-fi films from 2020 with a rating above 8") ```
**When it breaks:**
- **Adds ~200-400ms per query** for the LLM filter-generation step. High-latency tolerance required. - **Filter quality depends on `AttributeInfo` descriptions.** A vague description ("some number") produces no filter and falls back to pure vector search silently. - **Only works with stores that support pre-retrieval metadata filtering** — Chroma, Qdrant, pgvector, Pinecone. FAISS does not, so "only documents tagged topic:rag" is not possible without migrating. - **`enable_limit=True`** lets the LLM set how many results to return, but the generated limit overrides your default `k`. Test on your data before enabling. - **Multi-field OR logic** is not universally supported across translators. Check your store's translator for exact operator support before relying on OR conditions.
**Sources:** [LangChain how-to: Self-query retrieval](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/self_query) · [Chroma SelfQuery integration](https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/retrievers/self_query/chroma_self_query) · [MongoDB Atlas self-query tutorial](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/ai-integrations/langchain/self-query-retrieval/)

item.title: You Already Shipped the Component — Import the Repo Into Claude Design to Explore a Change Without Rebuilding From a Blank Canvas
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Link your GitHub repo in Claude Design's design system settings to start canvas explorations from your real components — not generic defaults. Use this when you need options before committing to a rework.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Link your GitHub repo in Claude Design's design system settings; explorations start from your real components, not generic defaults — the reverse round-trip for when you need three directions before committing to a rework.**
The Claude Design → Claude Code handoff gets written about constantly. The reverse direction — taking something that already lives in your repo back into Claude Design to explore a change — works through design system import and is what you reach for when a component needs visual exploration before you commit to rework.
**When this is useful:** - You want to try three layout directions on an existing feature without committing a diff - A stakeholder needs to see options, not a finished PR - You want Claude Design's generations to stay inside your component vocabulary instead of inventing new patterns
**How to set it up:**
In Claude Design, open the design system panel and link your repository. Claude Design reads your component exports, Tailwind config, and CSS tokens, using them as the generation context. You're no longer starting from a generic component library — you're starting from what your app already renders.
``` Claude Design → Design system panel → Link repository Paste your GitHub repo URL (must be public; use the file upload for private repos) ```
Once linked, any component Claude Design generates is checked against your component map before it appears. If your `Button` already exists in the repo, the generated output uses it rather than creating a new variant.
**Where the round-trip breaks:**
This is a one-way sync: Claude Design reads from the repo but doesn't push back automatically. Changes you make on the canvas are expressed as a new export bundle, not a diff against your component source. Use it for exploration and direction-setting, not for iterating on the actual implementation — that belongs in Claude Code once a direction is decided.
Private repos require a manual upload rather than a live GitHub link, which means the design system context goes stale as your repo evolves. For active development, run `/design-sync` in Claude Code to keep the local spec current, then re-upload when you need a new exploration round.
One further limit: Claude Design checks generated output against your component map, but it doesn't enforce your component API exactly — props may differ from your actual interface. Treat the output as a direction, not a finished component.

item.title: Claude Code Automatically Summarizes Sessions Left Idle 54 Minutes — Set idleCompaction: false or Raise the Threshold When That Loses Your Context
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Idle compaction runs just before the one-hour cache expires; it saves resume cost but can drop accumulated constraints. Disable in settings.json or tune the CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS threshold.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Claude Code auto-summarizes your session at 54 minutes idle to cut cache-resume cost — if that summary drops critical accumulated context, disable it with `"idleCompaction": false` in settings.json.**
Claude Code (v2.1.299, recently extended to the VS Code panel and desktop app's Code tab) added idle compaction: when a session sits idle for about 54 minutes, it automatically compacts the conversation just before the one-hour prompt cache expires. The goal is a cheaper resume — your next turn starts from a summary rather than re-sending the full history.
**Three things to know:** - Compaction triggers at the 54-minute mark if the session exceeds 200,000 tokens. Below that, the cache just expires and the next turn resumes cold. - The summary can silently drop detailed constraints you built up during the session — if you issued many inline rules or decision context over time, they may not survive compaction. - `CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS` lets you lower the threshold floor (minimum 100,000); no documented way to raise it above 200K.
**How to control it:**
Disable completely: ```json // .claude/settings.json { "idleCompaction": false } ```
Or via `/config` → "Idle compaction" row (requires v2.1.302+). Turning off `autoCompact` also disables idle compaction.
**When to disable:** - Sessions where you've built up specific constraints, file paths, or task state over time - Long-running background tasks where the session is waiting, not idle - Anytime you need the full history when you return
**When to leave it on:** - Exploration sessions with no critical accumulated state — you get a cheaper cold start - Short, focused tasks where any summary would include everything that matters
Note: one independent report suggests the env-var disable (`DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT`) had inconsistent behavior in an earlier version. If you need reliable disablement, use the settings.json approach and confirm it took effect in `/config`.
**Sources:** [What is Idle Compaction in Claude Code — claudelog.com](https://claudelog.com/faqs/what-is-idle-compaction-in-claude-code/) · [Claude Code Hub — idle compaction](https://wmedia.es/en/tips/claude-code-idle-compaction) · [dsebastien.net explainer](https://www.dsebastien.net/2026-10-16-claude-code-idle-compaction-cheaper-to-resume-but-from-a-summary/)

item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Add `User-agent: __usage_ai-training / Disallow: /` to your robots.txt now — Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic jointly committed on October 30 to honor it for training opt-out, with implementation starting 2027.**
On October 30, the four companies announced they will honor a shared robots.txt signal for AI training opt-out. The underlying mechanism is an IETF Internet-Draft authored by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley, adding a new policy token called `__usage_ai-training`.
**How to add it:**
``` User-agent: __usage_ai-training Disallow: / ```
Add this group to your robots.txt alongside any existing `ClaudeBot`, `GPTBot`, or `Google-Extended` entries. The signal tells all four labs not to use the matching paths for training, without having to maintain separate entries per crawler.
**Implementation timeline varies by company:** Anthropic says it has started. Microsoft gives February 1, 2027. Google and OpenAI give 2027 without a specific date.
**Limits to understand:** - This is a voluntary IETF draft, not a ratified standard — no enforcement mechanism exists. - The existing `User-agent: *` wildcard deliberately does not cover the new token; your current wildcard block does not substitute for the new group. - It has no effect on content already in existing training datasets — only future runs. - Each company's existing mechanism (`Google-Extended`, `ClaudeBot`, etc.) still works independently.
**Why it matters:** If you ship sites or APIs, adding this group is now the cross-vendor way to signal training opt-out for all four labs at once. Whether the signal holds long-term depends on each company's compliance — treat it as a reasonable-effort flag, not a legal guarantee.

item.title: Your Knowledge Base Re-Embeds Every Document Every Run — LangChain's Indexing API Tracks Source IDs and Skips Unchanged Files
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangChain's index() with SQLRecordManager skips unchanged chunks and removes stale ones — cleanup=incremental means only changed documents trigger new embedding API calls.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Wrap your vector store loads in LangChain's `index()` function with a `SQLRecordManager` — it hashes every chunk, skips unchanged ones, and deletes stale chunks from modified sources so your KB stays current without redundant embedding calls.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Keep a production knowledge base in sync with its source documents, paying for embedding API calls only when content actually changes.
**Three things to know:** - The record manager stores a content hash, write timestamp, and source ID per chunk — a re-run skips anything whose hash matches. - `cleanup="incremental"` removes chunks from sources seen in this run that were not updated — handles deletions and edits within active sources. - `cleanup="full"` removes anything not in the current run — use it for a complete refresh or when entire sources are removed from the corpus.
**The walkthrough:**
```bash pip install langchain-community langchain-openai ```
```python from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma from langchain.indexes import SQLRecordManager, index from langchain_core.documents import Document
# 1. Stand up the record manager (namespace = vectorstore + collection name) record_manager = SQLRecordManager( "chroma/my_docs", db_url="sqlite:///record_manager_cache.sql" ) record_manager.create_schema()
# 2. Connect to your vector store vectorstore = Chroma( collection_name="my_docs", embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings() )
# 3. Load your chunked documents — each needs a source metadata key docs = [ Document(page_content="...", metadata={"source": "docs/guide.md"}), Document(page_content="...", metadata={"source": "docs/api.md"}), ]
# 4. First run: writes both documents result = index(docs, record_manager, vectorstore, cleanup="incremental", source_id_key="source") # {"num_added": 2, "num_updated": 0, "num_skipped": 0, "num_deleted": 0}
# 5. Re-run with no changes: both chunks skipped, zero embedding calls result = index(docs, record_manager, vectorstore, cleanup="incremental", source_id_key="source") # {"num_added": 0, "num_updated": 0, "num_skipped": 2, "num_deleted": 0} ```
**Where it breaks:** - `cleanup="incremental"` only removes chunks from sources explicitly included in the current run. If a source file disappears from your corpus entirely and you don't include it in the run, its chunks survive in the vector store. For full deletions, switch to `cleanup="full"` for that run, or pass the source IDs to a manual delete. - The record manager state is separate from the vector store. If you drop and recreate the vector store without clearing the record manager, the manager thinks the chunks are already there and skips re-indexing them. Run `record_manager.create_schema()` fresh and do a full cleanup pass after any vector store reset. - `source_id_key` is required for `incremental` mode — the API raises `ValueError` if you omit it.
**Sources:** [How to reindex data to keep your vectorstore in sync — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/indexing) · [SQLRecordManager API reference — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/api_reference/_modules/langchain_core/indexing/api.html)

item.title: The Claude Design Export Bundle Tells Claude Code What It Looks Like, Not What It Calls — Add a 10-Line Wiring Brief to Tell It the Routes, API Endpoints, and State Layer
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The Claude Design export bundle carries layout and styling but not routes, API calls, or state. A short wiring brief in your handoff prompt prevents Claude Code from inventing a data layer.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: The Claude Design export gives Claude Code structure and styling — add one short section naming the route, the data calls, and the state layer so Claude Code doesn't guess the parts it can't see.**
The Claude Design export bundle carries what the tool knows: component layout, visual structure, design tokens, and styling. It does not carry what it can't see: which route the screen lives at, what API calls the components make, what state management layer you're using, or how the data flows between components.
Without that information, Claude Code makes plausible guesses — and those guesses often create technical debt: a new `useState` where you use React Query, a hardcoded fetch URL that won't match your backend, or a component dropped at `/new-screen` when it belongs at `/settings/notifications`.
**Add a wiring brief to your handoff prompt.** It doesn't need to be long:
``` Route: /settings/notifications Data: GET /api/user/notifications → { items: Notification[], unread: number } State: React Query, 2-min cache, mutation via PATCH /api/user/notifications/:id Parent: app/(authenticated)/settings/layout.tsx wraps with SettingsNav Auth: session already in context — no additional guard needed ```
Five lines prevent three common mistakes. Claude Code reads this and places the component on the right route, wires it to the right data hook, and doesn't invent a parallel fetch layer.
**What to include in the wiring brief:** 1. **Route** — the exact path, including dynamic segments 2. **Data** — the API call(s) and their return shapes (a one-line JSON schema is enough) 3. **State** — your state library and cache policy, so it uses the existing pattern 4. **Parent layout** — which wrapper component this screen lives inside 5. **Auth** — whether this route requires auth and how it's already handled
**The limit:** Claude Design has no access to your running API or codebase structure, so it can't derive any of this automatically. The wiring brief is manual work now. Future versions may read this from codebase context, but today the gap is real and worth closing yourself.

item.title: Your Edited Skill SKILL.md Needs a Session Restart to Take Effect — Run /reload-skills to Test Changes Without Closing the Session
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code hot-reloads skills from .claude/skills/ without a restart. The /reload-skills command confirms which skills were added, modified, or removed in the current session.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Changes to `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` take effect without restarting; run `/reload-skills` for an explicit rescan that shows exactly which skills changed.**
When you're writing a new skill or debugging an existing one, the old workflow was: edit the SKILL.md, close the session, restart, test. As of Claude Code v2.1.0, edits to `~/.claude/skills/` and `.claude/skills/` are hot-reloaded — the runtime picks them up automatically during normal message handling.
The `/reload-skills` command (added in v2.1.152) makes this explicit: it rescans both skill directories immediately and prints a summary of loaded, added, and removed skills. Use it when you want confirmation that your edit was picked up, or when you've edited several skills at once.
**Practical loop for skill development:**
1. Create `.claude/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md` with the skill's instructions 2. Test in the current session: invoke it and see what Claude does 3. Edit SKILL.md to refine 4. Run `/reload-skills` — confirm the update appears in the summary 5. Test again, without restarting
**One limit:** A brand-new *top-level* `skills/` directory (not yet inside `.claude/`) still requires a restart for Claude Code to discover it. Once a skill directory is known to the runtime, edits inside it hot-reload on the next message or `/reload-skills` call.
