item.title: Your Agent Resends the Whole Conversation Every Turn — Anthropic's Message Threads Beta Sends Only New Messages per Request
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic's message threads beta (Nov 2) lets agents send only new messages per turn instead of full history. Threads expire after 5 minutes and don't support Message Batches or token counting.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Message threads beta (beta header `message-threads-2026-08-12`) lets your agent send only new messages each turn instead of the full history; Anthropic reports ~35% lower time to first token on large requests.**
If your Claude agent sends the full `messages` array on every turn, you're re-transmitting and re-tokenizing the same context repeatedly. The new message threads beta changes this: add a `thread` parameter to your Messages API request, and the platform holds the conversation between turns. Each subsequent call sends only the new message, and the response includes a thread ID for the next turn.
The feature shipped November 2 and is [documented at platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/message-threads.md). It's available on the Claude API, AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, and GCP. Claude Code already uses it by default for most sessions.
**Limits to know before you use it:**
- Threads expire 5 minutes after the last request — your app still needs its own conversation history as a replay source; the platform holds state, but you hold the record - Not eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA use cases - Doesn't support Message Batches or the token counting API - The ~35% faster time-to-first-token figure is Anthropic's own benchmark on large requests, not independently verified
**Why it matters:** For agents running long multi-turn conversations, resending the full history is the dominant latency source on each turn. Threads move that cost off the critical path. Worth using in any agent harness where you're building the messages array manually — but keep your own copy: the thread expiry means the platform is not a durable conversation store.
**Sources:** [Anthropic message threads docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/message-threads.md) · [The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-claude-message-threads/) · [Unite.ai coverage](https://www.unite.ai/anthropic-launches-message-threads-beta-for-long-running-agents/)

item.title: Your Claude Code Slash Commands and Hooks Live in Three Separate READMEs Nobody Copies to New Repos — A Plugin Marketplace Bundle and `--scope project` Commit Them to `.claude/settings.json` for the Whole Team
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Install a Claude Code plugin at project scope and it writes to .claude/settings.json; commit that file and every teammate who trusts the repo gets the same slash commands, hooks, and MCP bindings.
item.content:encoded:
**A Claude Code plugin bundles slash commands, hooks, MCP configs, and subagent definitions into one installable unit; `--scope project` writes the install into `.claude/settings.json` so you commit it once and teammates get it when they trust the repo.**
Every project-specific Claude Code customization — the `/deploy` command, a `validate-blog.sh` PostToolUse hook, the Jira MCP config — currently lives in a file someone has to know about and manually copy to each repo. The plugin system changes that: a plugin is a directory with a `manifest.json` that bundles `commands/`, `hooks/`, `.mcp.json`, and `agents/` into a single installable unit. Install it at project scope and the entry lands in `.claude/settings.json`.
**Three scopes — one matters for team distribution:**
- `--scope user` (default): writes to `~/.claude/settings.json` — applies only to you - `--scope project`: writes to `.claude/settings.json` — commit it; teammates see it - `--scope local`: writes to `.claude/settings.local.json` — your override, not committed
**How to set it up:**
Register a marketplace (any git repo with a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`):
``` /plugin marketplace add owner/plugin-repo ```
Or add `extraKnownMarketplaces` directly in `.claude/settings.json` for project-wide automatic registration — anyone who opens the repo gets the registry without a separate command.
Install a plugin at project scope:
``` claude plugin install my-tools@my-marketplace --scope project ```
Or inside a session: `/plugin install my-tools@my-marketplace --scope project`.
Commit `.claude/settings.json`. When a teammate opens the repo and trusts the folder, Claude Code prompts them to install the configured plugins.
**What a plugin can bundle:**
- `commands/` — slash command `.md` definitions - `hooks/` — shell scripts wired to tool lifecycle events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, Notification) - `.mcp.json` — MCP server declarations scoped to the project - `agents/` — subagent CLAUDE.md configurations
**Real limit before you reach for this:** Auto-install on trust requires teammates to confirm the folder trust prompt. An independent test from July 2026 (dev.classmethod.jp) found only a folder-trust confirmation — not a per-plugin dialog — but that behavior may vary by Claude Code version and org plugin policy. Verify against your org's settings before treating it as zero-friction rollout.
**Sources:** [Plugin install docs — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/install) · [How to use Claude Code plugins — dev.to/thryx](https://dev.to/thryx/how-to-use-claude-code-plugins-install-from-a-marketplace-or-build-your-own-574) · [Team distribution test — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/articles/claude-code-plugin-team-distribution/)

item.title: Your SFT-Fine-Tuned Model Gets Facts Right But Doesn't Show Its Work — GRPO on a Free Colab T4 Trains Any 1B+ Model to Reason Step-by-Step Using Format Rewards, No Labeled Answer Dataset Required
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GRPO fine-tunes a model to reason step-by-step by rewarding format rather than correctness; the HuggingFace LLM Course Colab runs the full loop on Gemma 3 1B with Unsloth + LoRA on a free T4.
item.content:encoded:
**GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) fine-tunes a model to produce structured reasoning by rewarding format rather than answers — no labeled chain-of-thought dataset needed; the HuggingFace LLM Course exercise runs it on Gemma 3 1B with Unsloth + LoRA on a free Colab T4.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Take a base or SFT-trained model and fine-tune it to produce structured `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>` output before its final answers — without writing a labeled dataset of correct chain-of-thought. The reward functions score format, not content, so the model learns to externalise its thinking.
**Three things to take away:**
- GRPO is reinforcement learning without a separate reward model: the model generates multiple completions per prompt, your reward functions score them, and the update step pushes toward the higher-scoring half. You write the reward functions; they're plain Python. - Format rewards are the practical entry point: reward correct XML structure and penalise bare answers. The model learns the thinking structure and fills it in — you don't have to produce ground-truth reasoning traces. - Unsloth + QLoRA makes this feasible on free hardware: Gemma 3 1B at 4-bit loads in ~4 GB VRAM; a 3B model fits the same T4; the HuggingFace course exercise completes in under 30 minutes.
**Walk-through (HuggingFace LLM Course, Chapter 12 Exercise 6):**
```python from unsloth import FastLanguageModel model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( "google/gemma-3-1b-it", max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, ) model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=32, lora_alpha=32) ```
Define a reward function that scores XML format:
```python import re
def format_reward(completions, **kwargs): pattern = r"<reasoning>.*?</reasoning>\s*<answer>.*?</answer>" return [0.5 if re.search(pattern, c, re.DOTALL) else 0.0 for c in completions] ```
Pass it to `GRPOTrainer` from TRL:
```python from trl import GRPOTrainer, GRPOConfig
trainer = GRPOTrainer( model=model, reward_funcs=[format_reward], args=GRPOConfig(output_dir="grpo-output", max_steps=200), train_dataset=dataset, ) trainer.train() model.save_pretrained("grpo-reasoning-adapter") ```
The trainer generates N completions per prompt, scores each with `format_reward`, and updates toward the higher-scoring half. No labeled answers needed.
**Limits to know before you start:** Unsloth requires a base model of at least 1.5B parameters — smaller models don't reliably generate thinking tokens. Format rewards also get gamed: check that the content inside the tags is coherent, not just structurally correct. If the model stops improving, the [Unsloth advanced notebook](https://docs.unsloth.ai/basics/reasoning-grpo-and-rl) uses partial-credit reward functions that are harder to game.
**Sources:** [GRPO exercise — HuggingFace LLM Course Ch. 12.6](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/en/chapter12/6) · [GRPO + LoRA docs — docs.unsloth.ai](https://docs.unsloth.ai/basics/reasoning-grpo-and-rl) · [Train your own reasoning model — Unsloth tutorial](https://docs.unsloth.ai/basics/reasoning-grpo-and-rl/tutorial-train-your-own-reasoning-model-with-grpo) · [Gemma 3 GRPO walkthrough — youssefh.substack.com](https://youssefh.substack.com/p/gemma-3-reasoning-fine-tuning-with)

item.title: You Spend Three Iterations Fixing the Same Constraint Because It Was in Your Head, Not the Brief — Four Sections That Prevent Claude Design From Regenerating Your Defaults
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Structure your Claude Design brief with four sections—goal, constraints, components, anti-patterns—and your system rules land in the spec before the first generation, not after it.
item.content:encoded:
**Structure your Claude Design brief with four sections—goal, constraints, components, and anti-patterns—and your constraints are in the spec before the first generation, not discovered after three iterations.**
The common failure mode: you write "design a settings page" and spend three iterations correcting output because Claude Design used hardcoded `#3B82F6` instead of your `--color-primary`, a 12-column grid instead of your 8-column base, and wrapped everything in a sidebar you don't have. These corrections all lived in your head, not the brief.
**The four-section format**
Paste this into the Canvas description before the first generation:
``` ## Goal One sentence — what the user does on this screen. Example: "User reviews and updates notification preferences across three channels."
## Constraints Token names, grid spec, hard layout rules. Use exact names from your system. Example: Colors: --color-primary #0D9488, --color-surface #111827, --color-border #374151 Grid: 8-column, 24px gutter, 16px page margin Type: text-sm 14px, text-base 16px, font-sans (Inter)
## Components What Claude Code will use during handoff. Name the ones you have; ban the ones you don't. Example: Card, Button variant='contained', TextField, Switch from our MUI theme. Do NOT use Grid2 — use Box with flexbox.
## Anti-patterns The two or three things it keeps generating that don't belong. Example: No sidebar navigation. No purple. No full-bleed hero images. ```
**Why it works:** Claude Design reads the Canvas description before generating. Constraints in the description act as hard rails; anti-patterns flag deviations you've already seen. The first output still needs review, but the corrections shift from "wrong color, wrong grid, wrong nav" to fine-tuning alignment and spacing—changes that belong in the editor, not the canvas.
**When to update it:** When you change your token file or component library and notice drift on a new generation, update the Constraints section. A brief that references stale variable names is worse than no brief—Claude Design may confidently generate to outdated names, and Claude Code picks those up in the handoff.
**Real limit:** Complex layouts with many component interactions still drift, and components not in your brief's vocabulary can appear. The brief reduces iteration cycles; it does not eliminate them. For screens with more than five distinct component types, add a rough wire description to the Goal section alongside the task sentence—the additional layout signal matters.
**Sources:** [Claude Design developer guide — dev.to](https://dev.to/jangwook_kim_e31e7291ad98/claude-design-developer-guide-to-anthropics-prototyping-tool-1nc2), [Anthropic Labs Claude Design onboarding — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/), [Practitioner first-look: Claude Design — jwatte.com](https://jwatte.com/blog/blog-claude-design-anthropic-labs/)

item.title: Your Long Claude Code Session Degrades Silently as the Context Fills — Run `/compact` With a Preservation Hint Before Quality Drops, Not After
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code auto-compacts when the context fills, but /compact with a hint preserves what matters—file paths, known bugs, current task—instead of letting the model decide what to round off.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code auto-compacts when the context window fills, but a manual `/compact` with a hint preserves what matters—modified file paths, known bugs, the current task—instead of letting the model decide what to round off.**
When a session runs long—multiple files, several tool loops, accumulated debugging context—Claude Code auto-compacts at some point. The model writes a summary and discards the original messages. What it keeps and what it abstracts away is opaque.
You can trigger compaction manually before that happens, and you can tell it what to preserve:
``` /compact keep all modified file paths, known bugs, and the current task list ```
The compactor includes what you named verbatim. Compare the two outcomes:
Without a hint: *"We have been working on a Node.js project and making improvements."*
With `keep all modified file paths, known bugs, and the current task list`: *"Modified: src/api/auth.ts, src/db/session.ts. Known bug: refresh token race condition on concurrent logins (not fixed). Current task: add rate limiting to /api/login."*
**When to run it manually:** - Before shifting from a debugging phase to an implementation phase—the bug context needs to carry forward, but the diagnostic back-and-forth does not - When responses start hedging or re-asking questions you already answered - Proactively before the window fills, so you control the summary instead of auto-compact doing it at an arbitrary point
**Real limit:** The summary is still a summary. A subtle multi-file interaction you spent 30 minutes tracing will be abstracted. Before compacting, drop the key insight into a comment in the relevant file, or add a note to CLAUDE.md—compaction preserves the map, not the terrain.
`/clear` is better when you are starting a genuinely different task on a different part of the codebase—no prior context is useful, and compaction just carries noise forward.
**Sources:** [Claude Code docs — Memory and context](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/memory), [Claude Code changelog (context compaction controls, v2.1.293)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog), [Anthropic: Steering Claude Code (June 2026)](https://claude.com/blog/steering-claude-code-skills-hooks-rules-subagents-and-more)

item.title: Your Retrieved Chunks Are Half Irrelevant Text — Wrap Your Retriever in `ContextualCompressionRetriever` to Extract Only the Sentences That Answer the Query
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangChain's ContextualCompressionRetriever strips irrelevant sentences from each retrieved chunk before they reach your answer model—pair k=10 for recall, let the compressor handle precision.
item.content:encoded:
**LangChain's `ContextualCompressionRetriever` passes each retrieved chunk through an LLM that extracts only the relevant sentences, so your answer model gets 3 targeted sentences instead of 3 full paragraphs.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Route retrieved documents through a compression step that strips the sentences unrelated to the query, reducing the noise in your answer model's context window without cutting recall.
**Three things to take away:** - Compression trades latency for signal quality: one LLM call per retrieved document—use a Haiku-class model for the compressor, not Opus - `LLMChainExtractor` returns the relevant sentences; `LLMChainFilter` is binary—keep or drop the whole chunk - Set `k=10` on the base retriever to favor recall; let the compressor handle precision—this is the division of labor LangChain's own launch post describes
**Walk-through**
```python pip install langchain langchain-anthropic langchain-community chromadb ```
```python from langchain.retrievers.contextual_compression import ContextualCompressionRetriever from langchain.retrievers.document_compressors import LLMChainExtractor from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from langchain_chroma import Chroma
# Use a fast, cheap model for the compression pass—not your answer model llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-5-5", temperature=0) compressor = LLMChainExtractor.from_llm(llm)
base_retriever = Chroma( collection_name="docs", embedding_function=your_embedding_fn, ).as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 10})
compression_retriever = ContextualCompressionRetriever( base_compressor=compressor, base_retriever=base_retriever, )
docs = compression_retriever.invoke("How do I configure the request timeout?") for doc in docs: print(doc.page_content) # 1–4 sentences, not a full chunk ```
Before compression, a question about a single config key returns chunks that mention it in three different contexts, each surrounded by unrelated setup steps. After compression, you get the sentences that state the value and explain it—and those are what the answer model reasons over.
**Real limits:** - At one LLM call per retrieved document with `k=10`, that is 10 extra inference calls per query. LangChain runs them serially by default; use `ainvoke` if latency matters. - `LLMChainExtractor` can return an empty string if none of a chunk's sentences are relevant. Your downstream code must handle empty `page_content`. - The compressor can over-extract when chunks are dense—a sentence about timeouts might include the surrounding dependency context that the extractor drops. Watch for answers that are technically correct but miss the "why."
**Sources:** [LangChain how-to: Contextual compression](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/contextual_compression), [LangChain blog: Improving Document Retrieval with Contextual Compression](https://blog.langchain.com/improving-document-retrieval-with-contextual-compression)

item.title: Your Generated Components Use Tailwind Defaults When Your Design System Lives in a File Claude Code Has Never Seen — A CLAUDE.md Reference Puts Your Tokens in Every Session
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Generated components drift from your design system because Claude Code's session starts without your token file. A docs/design-tokens.md + one CLAUDE.md line fixes the drift.
item.content:encoded:
**Generated components drift from your design system because Claude Code's session starts without your token file. A `docs/design-tokens.md` + one CLAUDE.md line fixes the drift.**
When you hand off a Claude Design export to Claude Code for landing in your codebase, the new components it generates for nearby features often drift: `blue-500` where your system says `primary-600`, generic spacing where your base-8 scale lives. The export brought the component structure; it didn't bring your token vocabulary.
**Make your token spec readable**
Create `docs/design-tokens.md` with your resolved values — not your Tailwind config, which Claude Code can't execute, but the computed output:
```markdown ## Colors - primary-600: #2563eb - primary-700: #1d4ed8 - surface-0: #ffffff - surface-1: #f9fafb - neutral-800: #1f2937
## Spacing (base-8) - space-1: 8px space-2: 16px space-3: 24px space-4: 32px
## Type scale - size-sm: 14px size-base: 16px size-lg: 18px size-xl: 20px - font-sans: "Inter", system-ui ```
If your tokens go through a `withOpacity()` helper or custom Tailwind plugin, run `npx tailwindcss --input globals.css > resolved.css` and pull out the custom properties — that's what Claude Code can actually read.
**Tell Claude Code where to look**
Add one section to `CLAUDE.md`:
```markdown ## Design system Before generating any UI component, read docs/design-tokens.md. Use these tokens for all colors, spacing, and type — never inline Tailwind utilities not mapped here. ```
From this point, every generation request starts from your vocabulary, not training-data defaults.
**Where it breaks down:** aliases (`--color-primary: var(--color-brand-base)`) can resolve incompletely — Claude Code reads the spec, not your PostCSS pipeline. Flatten to hex/px values for reliability. The file also drifts if your design system evolves and you don't update it; treat it as a maintained artifact alongside your theme config.
**Sources:** [Design Systems Collective: Using Claude Code as a design system designer](https://www.designsystemscollective.com/how-i-use-claude-code-agent-with-vs-code-as-a-design-system-designer-541e105c0c97), [claudify.tech: CLAUDE.md for Tailwind design systems](https://claudify.tech/blog/claude-code-tailwind), [combray.prose.sh: Capturing your design system for AI editors](https://combray.prose.sh/2025-11-28-design-system-capture-best-practices)

item.title: Your Claude Code Agent Waits to Be Summoned — Wire a Webhook to `claude -p` and Let Any External Event Trigger an Autonomous Response
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Parse a webhook payload, assemble context, run claude -p non-interactively, route the output back. Three constraints make it reliable in unattended mode: self-contained prompts, --max-turns cap, and minimum --allowedTools.
item.content:encoded:
**Parse any webhook event into a context-rich prompt, run `claude -p` non-interactively, and route the output back — Claude acts when events happen, without you at the keyboard.**
DeepSeek's [Super-Agent prototype](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent) (covered earlier today) monitors team chats and acts without being summoned. The same pattern is available today with `claude -p`: a three-step pipeline turns any external event into an autonomous Claude action.
**Step 1 — Receive and parse the event**
A webhook handler (a Modal function, a Vercel serverless route, any HTTP endpoint) receives the payload and extracts what Claude needs. For a GitHub PR review comment:
```bash REPO_NAME="$(jq -r .repository.full_name <<< "$PAYLOAD")" PR_NUMBER="$(jq -r .pull_request.number <<< "$PAYLOAD")" COMMENT_BODY="$(jq -r .comment.body <<< "$PAYLOAD")" COMMENT_AUTHOR="$(jq -r .comment.user.login <<< "$PAYLOAD")" ```
**Step 2 — Assemble a self-contained prompt**
Claude can't ask clarifying questions in headless mode, so the prompt must be complete on its own. Include paths, error text, and exact context:
```bash PROMPT=$(cat <<EOF REPO: $REPO_NAME PR: #$PR_NUMBER AUTHOR: $COMMENT_AUTHOR COMMENT: $COMMENT_BODY
Task: If this comment requests a specific code change, apply it and run the tests. If it asks a question, answer directly from the code. Be concise. EOF ) ```
**Step 3 — Run Claude and route the response**
```bash RESPONSE=$(echo "$PROMPT" \ | claude -p \ --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(pnpm test:*)" \ --max-turns 6 \ --output-format text 2>&1)
# Route back to GitHub gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" \ --repo "$REPO_NAME" \ --body "$RESPONSE" ```
**Three things that make this reliable in unattended mode:**
1. **Self-contained prompts over lazy delegation.** "Look at the PR and fix things" gives Claude nothing to work with. Include the exact comment text, relevant file paths, and any error output — the prompt is the only context it has. 2. **Cap turns with `--max-turns`.** A runaway loop on every webhook is expensive. 4–8 turns handles most event-response tasks; raise it only for complex multi-file changes. 3. **Scope `--allowedTools` to the minimum.** A PR comment responder needs `Read`, `Edit`, and maybe `Bash(pnpm test:*)`. Never give unattended agents unrestricted `Bash`.
**Limits to know before you ship this:**
- **Latency.** `claude -p` starts a full session; median response is 5–20 seconds. Don't use it where callers expect a sub-second reply (Slack slash commands, interactive UIs). - **Cost at volume.** Each event fires a session with full context. Rate-limit or deduplicate high-frequency event sources before wiring Claude to them. - **No interactive approval.** Design every action to be reversible — Claude cannot pause to ask you whether to proceed. Prefer `Edit` over `Bash(git push:*)` and let a human merge the result.

item.title: Your Document Splitter Cuts Mid-Sentence Because It Counts Characters — `SemanticChunker` Embeds Sentences First and Splits Where Meaning Actually Shifts
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: SemanticChunker embeds every sentence, computes similarity deltas between neighbors, and places splits where the delta exceeds a percentile threshold — topic boundaries instead of byte counts.
item.content:encoded:
**LangChain's `SemanticChunker` embeds consecutive sentences, measures how much meaning changes between them, and places splits at the biggest semantic jumps — not at a fixed character count.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** split a multi-topic document so each chunk covers one coherent idea, rather than ending mid-argument because you hit 500 characters.
**Three things to know before you run it:**
1. **How the split decision works.** Every pair of adjacent sentences is embedded; the cosine distance between neighbors is computed. The splitter ranks all those distances, picks the ones above a chosen percentile (default: the 95th), and places a boundary there. A 70th-percentile threshold produces more, smaller chunks; 95th produces fewer, larger ones. 2. **Four threshold types; start with `percentile`.** The API exposes `percentile`, `standard_deviation`, `interquartile`, and `gradient`. `percentile` at 90–95 is the safest default for general documents. Gradient is adaptive but less predictable until you know your content. 3. **It lives in `langchain_experimental` — not the core package.** Treat that as a stability caveat: the API may change, and it isn't enabled by default even with `langchain` installed.
**Walk-through:**
```bash pip install langchain-experimental langchain-huggingface sentence-transformers ```
```python from langchain_experimental.text_splitter import SemanticChunker from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
splitter = SemanticChunker( embeddings, breakpoint_threshold_type="percentile", breakpoint_threshold_amount=90, # split at the top 10% of semantic jumps )
docs = splitter.create_documents([your_text]) # docs is a list of Document objects, each with page_content and metadata print(f"{len(docs)} chunks") for i, d in enumerate(docs): print(f"Chunk {i}: {len(d.page_content)} chars — {d.page_content[:80]}…") ```
Swap in any embedding model — `OpenAIEmbeddings()` works the same way; just note it calls the API for every sentence.
**When NOT to use it:**
- **Large corpora.** Every sentence in the document gets embedded. A 100-page PDF may spend 30–90 seconds in this splitter. For anything that needs to run quickly at scale, fall back to `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`. - **Structured documents.** Code files, Markdown with explicit sections, CSVs, and tables chunk better by structural delimiter than by semantic shift. `SemanticChunker` has nothing to act on when the "meaning" is in the schema, not the prose. - **Short texts.** If most of your documents are under 500 words, `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` at an appropriate chunk size produces almost the same result at a fraction of the cost.
**Sources:** [SemanticChunker tutorial — LangChain Open Tutorial](https://langchain-opentutorial.gitbook.io/langchain-opentutorial/07-textsplitter/04-semanticchunker) · [SemanticChunker API reference — LangChain experimental](https://python.langchain.com/api_reference/experimental/text_splitter/langchain_experimental.text_splitter.SemanticChunker.html) · [RAG chunking strategies compared — machinelearningplus.com](https://machinelearningplus.com/?p=26308)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Signs Off Before Your Tests Pass — A Stop Hook That Exits 2 Blocks Completion and Sends Claude Back, With One Environment Check to Prevent an Infinite Loop
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A Stop hook runs every time Claude tries to end its turn. Exit 2 blocks completion and sends it back; check CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_ACTIVE first or the loop never ends. Concrete test-gate in 15 lines.
item.content:encoded:
**A Stop hook that exits 2 sends Claude back for another attempt; checking `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_ACTIVE` is the one thing that keeps it from looping forever.**
Your Claude Code session decides it's done whenever it runs out of obvious next steps — before you've confirmed whether the tests pass, the build is green, or the required output file was written. A **Stop hook** is how you add that gate.
A Stop hook runs every time Claude tries to end its turn. Two exit codes matter:
- **Exit 0:** all good — let it finish. - **Exit 2:** blocked — Claude reads your `reason` JSON from stdout and goes back for another pass.
**The one guard you cannot skip — `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_ACTIVE`**
Without this check, a hook that always exits 2 traps Claude in an infinite retry loop. The environment variable is set to `"1"` when a Stop hook is already blocking the current attempt — checking it first lets you fail open on the second pass and end the turn even if the check is still failing.
**Wire it up:**
```json // .claude/settings.json { "hooks": { "Stop": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "bash .claude/hooks/run-gate.sh" }] }] } } ```
```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # .claude/hooks/run-gate.sh
# Fail open if a previous Stop hook already blocked this turn. # Without this, a failing test traps Claude in an infinite retry loop. if [ "$CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_ACTIVE" = "1" ]; then exit 0 fi
# Run your fast check — keep this under the hook timeout (~60 s). if ! pnpm test --silent 2>&1; then printf '{"decision":"block","reason":"Test suite failed — fix before completing."}\n' exit 2 fi ```
Claude reads the JSON from stdout when exit 2 fires and feeds the `reason` back into the session. If the tests fail, Claude tries again. Once they pass (or after the first block), `exit 0` lets it finish.
**What gates work well here:**
- **Fast unit tests:** `pnpm test --silent` or `pytest -x -q`. Skip long integration suites — the hook timeout is 60 seconds. - **Lint as a gate:** `eslint --max-warnings 0` catches new violations Claude introduced in its last edit. - **File existence:** confirm a required output was written before sign-off: `[ -f dist/bundle.js ] || exit 2`.
**Limits:** Stop hooks run in the shell environment and cannot see what Claude is thinking — only what exists on disk. If the test failure is in a module Claude didn't realize it affected, the loop may not converge. The default retry cap is 8 blocks (`CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`). Design the gate check to be idempotent and fast; a hook that takes 45 seconds delays every turn end.
**Sources:** [Stop hooks reference — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/customization/hooks) · [Stop hook task enforcement — claudefa.st](https://claudefa.st/blog/tools/hooks/stop-hook-task-enforcement) · [Deep dive: Stop hooks and the self-validation loop — besthub.dev](https://besthub.dev/articles/deep-dive-into-claude-code-hooks-stop-hooks-and-the-self-validation-loop-a3dfdda1397b)

item.title: DeepSeek Open-Sources a Coding Agent That Monitors Your Team's Chat Without Being Summoned — A Research Prototype, but the Autonomous-Trigger Architecture Is Worth Watching
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: DeepSeek released Super-Agent under MIT license on November 1: an autonomous coding agent that watches developer group chats for coding issues and proposes fixes without being invoked.
item.content:encoded:
**DeepSeek released Super-Agent on November 1 — an MIT-licensed prototype of an autonomous coding agent that monitors developer group chats and proposes fixes without being explicitly invoked.**
DeepSeek published [Super-Agent](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent) (`dsh-superagent` on GitHub) as a research prototype explicitly aimed at competing with Claude Code. The distinctive design: instead of responding to explicit commands, it watches group chat conversations among developers, detects coding issues in the discussion, and suggests solutions on its own.
DeepSeek calls it "not an official DeepSeek product" — a research prototype with no guaranteed stability or support.
**Why it matters:** Claude Code and most coding agents operate on explicit invocation — you ask, they act. Super-Agent's trigger model is different: it monitors ambient conversation and intervenes when it judges the moment is right. The hard engineering problem here isn't the code generation (that's table stakes); it's knowing *when to interrupt*. Getting the trigger detection wrong produces either a useless agent that never fires or an annoying one that fires constantly. The MIT license means you can fork and retune the interrupt logic — which is more interesting than the prototype status suggests.
**Limit:** It is a research prototype. The trigger detection is almost certainly rough at this stage, and deploying it in an active team chat without significant tuning risks it firing on every debugging thread. The architecture is worth watching; the current release is not production-ready.

item.title: Anthropic's November 12 Policy Update Adds a Kill-Switch Requirement for Claude Controlling Hardware and Mandates Human Review for Hiring, Loan, and Medical AI Decisions
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Effective Nov 12: Claude connected to hardware must have a qualified operator able to observe and halt it. High-risk domains (hiring, loans, medical) need human review plus AI-use disclosure.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic's 2026 usage policy update (effective November 12 — ten days away) adds explicit requirements for Claude controlling hardware and for high-risk automated decisions in hiring, lending, and healthcare.**
Announced October 8, this update is separate from the [Democratic Processes section](https://www.anthropic.com/news/election-safeguards-update) covered earlier. It adds obligations for commercial and API deployments that make autonomous decisions or control physical systems.
**Physical actions (new):** When Claude controls hardware capable of causing physical harm, a qualified operator must be present and able to observe and stop the equipment at any time. The system must maintain a safe state if Claude disconnects. This applies to robots, industrial equipment, and any autonomous machinery where Claude drives the control loop.
**High-risk automated decisions (clarified with new specificity):** Candidate screening, loan pricing, medical advice, and financial recommendations now explicitly require: 1. A qualified human reviewer who can inspect and modify the output before it reaches the affected person. 2. Disclosure to that person that AI was involved in the decision.
**Agents and browser automation:** Users who build or deploy agents — including actions taken through tools, browsers, or connected systems — are responsible for ensuring those agents comply with the policy.
**Limit:** Anthropic describes most changes as clarifications of existing rules, not new obligations. Third-party coverage conflicts on whether the requirements cover all deployments or only consumer-facing outputs — read the [official policy text](https://anthropic.com/aup) directly before drawing compliance conclusions.
**Why it matters:** If you are deploying Claude via Bedrock or the API in any automated-decision or hardware-control context, November 12 is your deadline to confirm you have the required human oversight in place.

item.title: Your Inference Code Has a Separate SDK Setup Per Provider — OpenRouter Puts 200+ Models Behind One OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint and Lets You Define Fallback Chains in the Request
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: OpenRouter exposes any major hosted model through one OpenAI-compatible base_url. Declare a models fallback list in extra_body and the response field shows which provider actually served the call.
item.content:encoded:
**OpenRouter gives you one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for 200+ hosted models — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen — with per-request fallback chains so a provider outage doesn't take your app down.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** call any major hosted model through your existing OpenAI SDK setup, declare ordered fallback providers in the same request, and log which provider actually served each call.
- Model names follow `provider/model-id` format: `anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5`, `openai/gpt-4o-mini`, `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct`. - OpenRouter's API is a drop-in: change `base_url` and pass your OpenRouter key. Every existing chat completion call works unchanged. - Fallback chains go in `extra_body` — the OpenAI SDK doesn't expose that field in its typed interface, so you pass it as a dict.
**Setup:**
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key="your-openrouter-key", # from openrouter.ai/keys )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this pull request diff."}], extra_body={ # If Claude Haiku is unavailable, fall through to Llama on Together AI. "models": [ "anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5", "meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct", ], "route": "fallback", }, )
# Which provider actually served this call? print(response.model) # e.g. "meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct" on fallback ```
**`openrouter/auto` — handle with care.** Setting `model="openrouter/auto"` lets OpenRouter choose per prompt. It works but tends to underestimate task complexity and select cheaper models; independent testing has found it reaches for lower-capacity options more often than expected. Use it in prototyping; for production, declare explicit fallback chains.
**Check current model availability and pricing** at [openrouter.ai/models](https://openrouter.ai/models) — the catalog changes and listed prices can differ significantly between providers for the same model.
**Limits:** OpenRouter is a meta-router, not a model provider — it resells capacity from underlying providers. Pricing has two layers (the provider rate plus OpenRouter's margin). Latency has an extra network hop. Rate limits are set by the underlying provider, not by OpenRouter, so high-throughput workloads can still hit per-provider ceilings. For maximum throughput or minimum latency, calling a provider directly is faster and cheaper. OpenRouter is the right tool for prototyping across models, building resilience against provider outages, or consolidating multiple provider accounts into one SDK setup.
**Sources:** [OpenRouter docs — openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/docs) · [OpenRouter API tutorial — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/openrouter) · [Together vs OpenRouter vs Fireworks — earlier in this series](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-22-01-together-ai-openai-sdk-base-url-open-models)

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Still Has 400 Lines of Rules a Claude 5 Model Doesn't Need — Move Knowledge to Skills, Replace Instructions With Tools, Keep Only Gotchas
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: For Claude 5 models, Anthropic reports cutting over 80% of Claude Code's built-in system prompt. Your CLAUDE.md should follow: move rules to skills, replace instructions with tools, keep only gotchas.
item.content:encoded:
**For Claude 5 models, Anthropic (per its July 2026 guidance) reports cutting over 80% of Claude Code's built-in system prompt — replacing explicit rules with model judgment. Your CLAUDE.md should follow the same pattern.**
**Three shifts that improve Claude Code sessions immediately:**
**1. Replace rules with judgment.** Your CLAUDE.md likely has lines like "Always add error handling for API calls" or "Never use `var` in TypeScript." Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 already apply these conventions correctly without being told. Writing them as rules wastes tokens and, worse, forces the model to pattern-match against rules rather than think. Run this audit and move or delete every match:
```bash # Find rule candidates to move out of CLAUDE.md: grep -nE "^[-*] (Always|Never|Do not|Make sure|Use .* for)" CLAUDE.md ```
**2. Move knowledge to skills; keep only gotchas in the root CLAUDE.md.** A skill at `.claude/skills/testing/SKILL.md` loads only when Claude is doing testing work. A 400-line root CLAUDE.md loads into every turn — including the ones where you are fixing a Worker with no relation to testing. Per the Anthropic guidance, target the root under ~80 lines:
``` # CLAUDE.md — keep this file to things that would surprise a senior engineer: # gotchas, non-obvious constraints, unusual build steps # # Move out: # testing conventions → @.claude/skills/testing/ # API patterns → @.claude/skills/api/ # architecture rules → @docs/claude/architecture.md ```
**3. Give Claude a tool instead of an instruction.** "Check the design system before choosing colors" is always-on context that often gets ignored mid-session. A tool that reads `design-tokens.json` on demand is better — Claude calls it when it needs color values and skips it otherwise. If information only matters sometimes, it belongs in a lazily loaded tool, not always-on context.
**Limits:** This calibration is for the Claude 5 family (Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Haiku 5, Fable 5.1). On Claude 4 models (Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.8), explicit rules still provide measurable guidance — the capability level is the prerequisite. Reduce your CLAUDE.md gradually: remove a section, run real sessions, verify behavior before removing the next.

item.title: The Claude Design Export Bundle Carries the Component Map But Not Your API — One Line Before the Handoff Prompt Points Claude Code to Your Actual Components
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The Claude Design handoff bundle contains a component map and design tokens but not your component API. One priming sentence before the bundle prompt points Claude Code to your actual library instead of shadcn defaults.
item.content:encoded:
**The export bundle carries your component map and design tokens — one sentence in the handoff prompt tells Claude Code which library to use instead of defaulting to shadcn.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Get the Claude Design export bundle into Claude Code and prime it to use your component library - Understand what the bundle contains (and what it deliberately omits) - Know when to go back to Claude Design vs. when to iterate in Claude Code
---
When you click Export → "Hand off to Claude Code" in Claude Design, the bundle contains: - A machine-readable component structure (which elements are containers, buttons, cards, lists) - Color tokens, typography, and spacing values used in the design - Layout hierarchy and component states you specified - A README and a pre-written prompt to paste into Claude Code
**What the bundle does not contain:** your component library's API. Claude Code knows a `Button[primary]` belongs here, but it has no idea whether your button is `<Button variant="primary">`, `<PrimaryButton>`, or `<btn class="btn-primary">`. Without a hint, it defaults to whatever library it associates with your stack.
**One sentence closes that gap.** Before pasting the bundle prompt, add:
``` Implement this design using the existing React components in src/components/. Do not introduce any new component library or install new packages. For unfamiliar component names, check src/components/index.ts. ```
**The handoff flow:**
1. Complete the design canvas in Claude Design (a full viewport, not a sketch). 2. Click Export → "Hand off to Claude Code." 3. Open Claude Code at your repo root. 4. Paste your component-library sentence, then paste the bundle prompt Claude Design generated. 5. Claude Code downloads the bundle, reads the component map and tokens, and starts implementing.
**When to go back to Claude Design:** when layout, information hierarchy, or the interaction model needs to change. When only implementation details need adjustment — correct props, event handlers, responsive variants — stay in the editor. The fastest convergence happens when each tool handles the layer it understands.
**Limits:** The bundle URL is temporary; download the `.zip` for long-lived work. Even with the priming sentence, Claude Code cannot infer your component prop names or variant signature — review generated prop usage against your actual interface. The handoff works best from a linked codebase (connect it in Claude Design settings) so the canvas has already tried to match your tokens.
**Sources:** [Using Claude Design for prototypes and UX — claude.com](https://claude.com/resources/tutorials/using-claude-design-for-prototypes-and-ux) · [Claude Design → Claude Code handoff guide — claude-code-playbook.pages.dev](https://claude-code-playbook.pages.dev/en/docs/level-4/claude-design-handoff) · [Get started with Claude Design — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design)

item.title: Generate Three Rough Directions in Claude Design Before Writing a Line of Code — The Comparison Becomes the Constraint Brief Your Claude Code Session Needs
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Generating three architecturally distinct directions in Claude Design before coding externalizes layout and hierarchy choices. The comparison note becomes the constraint brief Claude Code needs to generate on-brand, on-spec components.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Three design directions from Claude Design in 15 minutes surface layout and hierarchy conflicts you'd otherwise discover in code — and the comparison produces a constraint brief Claude Code can act on directly.**
When you jump straight to implementation, you commit to implicit decisions — layout, information density, interaction model — without ever examining them. A short exploration in Claude Design, before any code is written, externalizes those choices and makes them negotiable.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Generate three architecturally distinct directions for a feature from a single brief - Extract the surviving decisions as a constraint brief - Pass that brief to Claude Code and get components that stay within the chosen system
**The workflow**
Write a brief — 3–5 lines: what the feature does, who uses it, the one job it needs to do well, and the constraints (existing component library, color system, target screen sizes). In Claude Design (or a Claude artifact), ask for three distinct directions, not variations of one:
> "Generate three distinct UI directions for [feature brief]. Make them architecturally different — different information hierarchy, different interaction model, not just different colors. Label each by its tradeoff: e.g., 'dense / scannable', 'guided / linear', 'ambient / low-interrupt'."
Once you have three, write a comparison note: what each gets right, what it sacrifices, where each breaks. **That comparison is the spec.** The decisions that survive — "we need scannable density; primary action in one tap; use our existing Card and Button primitives" — become the constraint brief.
Hand that brief directly to Claude Code:
> "You're building [feature]. Constraints: [surviving list]. Components available: [library]. Generate the component tree starting with the container layout."
The exploration took 15 minutes; the brief took five; Claude Code works from a concrete spec rather than a vague description.
**Limits**: Claude Design explores layouts and hierarchy well but has no knowledge of your existing components unless you describe them. Generated directions tend toward clean, low-density layouts — if density matters, prompt for it explicitly. This workflow is strongest before the first line of code, not during iteration on something already built.

item.title: Your Whole Workflow Runs at Session Effort Because There's No Per-Process Override — CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK Ship in v2.1.316
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: v2.1.316 ships two cost controls: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT sets a process-level default effort for all subagents; CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK removes the keyword-triggered extended thinking for managed installs.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Claude Code v2.1.316 (Oct 31) ships two cost-control env vars — `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT` caps subagent effort at the process level, and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK` removes the keyword shortcut for managed or unattended installs.**
**CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT**
Before v2.1.316, every subagent inherited the parent session's effort level. A session running at `xhigh` for complex reasoning also spawned file-read subagents at `xhigh` — paying full-effort inference for tasks that don't need it. Setting `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT` in the environment overrides that default for all subagents in the process:
```bash # In your CI environment or .env: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT=medium # low | medium | high | xhigh | max ```
The parent session still runs at whatever effort you specified there. Only subagents change. Useful for: unattended CI runs where the orchestrator needs max context but workers do scoped, well-defined tasks; shared team installations where you want a cost ceiling by default.
**CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK**
`ultrathink` typed in a prompt triggers extended thinking at xhigh effort for that turn. It's a useful interactive shortcut but can fire accidentally in managed installs when a user pastes a log, a commit message, or a doc that happens to contain the word. Setting `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK=1` disables the keyword trigger entirely — extended thinking is still available via the session `effort` setting, just not via this shortcut.
```bash CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK=1 ```
**Limit:** `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT` is a default, not a ceiling — a subagent's own `effort:` frontmatter or an explicit `effort` parameter in an Agent tool call still takes precedence. Use it to lower the floor on un-configured subagents, not to cap carefully tuned ones.
**Timing:** Opus 4.8 Fast Mode retires November 30. If you have workflows that rely on fast-mode costs, now is the right time to audit effort settings and migrate to Opus 5.5 before the deadline.
**Sources:** [Claude Code 2.1.316: subagent effort becomes a setting, ultrathink gets a kill switch — dev.to/piekwerk](https://dev.to/piekwerk/claude-code-21316-subagent-effort-becomes-a-setting-ultrathink-gets-a-kill-switch-and-opus-16e) · [Claude Code model config — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config) · [clauding.de v2.1.316 walkthrough](https://clauding.de/en/posts/claude-code-2-1-316-ultrathink-subagent-effort/)

item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon ranks #1 on the AI Index but has no confirmed public API date. Anthropic retires Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.8 Fast Mode on November 30 — check your model strings today.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Google's new top model tops the benchmark tables but isn't publicly accessible via API yet; Anthropic's November 30 retirement deadline is 30 days out.**
**Gemini 4 Carbon**
Google DeepMind [announced Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/) on October 28. It ranks #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 (score: 59) and leads Google's published cyber benchmarks (SEC-bench Pro 88.2%, ExploitGym 54.8%, CWE-bench 71.0% — Google's own figures, not independently verified). On FrontierSWE 2 its 61.2% coding score trails Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, so the gap with Anthropic on code isn't closed. API pricing is listed at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, but [VentureBeat reports](https://venturebeat.com/technology/google-unveils-gemini-4-carbon-retaking-the-worlds-no-1-spot-on-updated-harder-benchmarks-but-access-is-limited) the public API endpoint isn't yet available and no date has been announced.
**Why it matters:** Carbon is on the developer path (AI Studio preview + Fairwind cybersecurity program), but wait for a confirmed public API before updating your routing configs.

item.title: Your Vector Store Uses the Same HNSW Parameters as a Tutorial Project — Three Numbers Control Recall and Latency at Production Scale
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: HNSW's m, ef_construction, and query ef are the three parameters that determine whether your vector search finds the right results and how fast it answers. Here's what each does and how to tune them in pgvector and Qdrant.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: HNSW's default parameters are tuned for small demo datasets — at production scale, three numbers (`m`, `ef_construction`, and query `ef`) control whether your vector search finds the right documents and how quickly it returns.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Understand what each HNSW parameter actually controls - Set `m` and `ef_construction` at index-build time to match your corpus size and accuracy requirement - Tune query `ef` in production to trade recall for latency
**What HNSW actually does**
Hierarchical Navigable Small World is a graph-based approximate nearest neighbor index. At build time, each vector is linked to its nearest neighbors across multiple layers. At query time, the search starts at an entry point and walks the graph, keeping the `ef` best candidates it has seen, stopping when no better neighbor can be found.
**The three parameters**
- **`m`** (connections per node, default: 16): higher `m` means a denser graph, better recall, and faster search — but more memory. `m=16` works well up to ~100K vectors. For corpora over 1M documents, consider `m=24–32`. Memory scales roughly as `O(m × n)`. - **`ef_construction`** (build-time candidate list size, default varies 64–128): higher means a higher-quality graph and better recall at query time — but a slower index build. It has no effect at query time. 128 is a reasonable starting point; 200–300 for high-accuracy requirements. - **`ef` (query-time candidate list, default varies)**: the live recall/latency dial. Higher `ef` → better recall, slower queries. Requires `ef >= top_k`; a common starting point is `ef = 2 × top_k`.
**In pgvector:**
```sql -- Create index with custom parameters CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 128);
-- Tune query ef per session or globally SET hnsw.ef_search = 100; ```
**In Qdrant:**
```python client.create_collection( collection_name="docs", vectors_config=VectorParams(size=768, distance=Distance.COSINE), hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff( m=16, ef_construct=128, full_scan_threshold=10000 # below this size, use exact search ) ) # At query time, pass ef via SearchParams client.query_points( "docs", query=query_vector, search_params=models.SearchParams(hnsw_ef=100) ) ```
**Limits**: Doubling `m` roughly doubles index memory — profile before scaling up. HNSW tuning can't fix a retrieval problem caused by bad chunking or wrong embedding model; get those right first. And `ef_construction` is a build-time setting — you can't change it without re-indexing.
**Sources:** [pgvector HNSW documentation — github.com/pgvector/pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#hnsw) · [Qdrant HNSW optimization guide — qdrant.tech](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/guides/optimize/) · [HNSW explained — pinecone.io/learn](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/series/faiss/hnsw/)

item.title: Your Single Agent Does Everything Itself Until Context Balloons — A LangGraph Supervisor Delegates via Tool Calls to Specialist Workers That Each See Their Own Slice
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Wire a LangGraph supervisor that hands off tasks to specialist workers via tool calls; each worker sees only its own message slice, keeping context tight.
item.content:encoded:
**Your single ReAct agent handles everything — and at some point its context fills with every prior sub-task and it starts confusing its own steps. A supervisor that delegates via tool calls gives each specialist its own clean context window.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Build a multi-agent graph where a supervisor routes tasks to specialist workers by calling tools; each worker sees only its own input, not the accumulated history of every prior delegation.
- A supervisor is a `create_react_agent` that treats each worker as a **tool** — it calls `transfer_to_researcher(query)` or `transfer_to_writer(draft)` rather than invoking the workers directly, which means the LLM decides when and how to delegate - Each worker is a compiled sub-graph or a plain Python function; wrapping it as a `@tool` is the only coupling point — change the worker internals without touching the supervisor - Three limits to build around: workers cannot see each other's state directly (the supervisor relays); the supervisor loops until `END` is reached (add `recursion_limit` to the config); and graph state is in-memory only — add a LangGraph checkpointer if you need persistence across requests
**Walk-through:**
```python from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from langchain_core.tools import tool from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-opus-5-5")
# --- specialist workers (each gets its own message slice) ---
def _run_researcher(query: str) -> str: agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools=[]) # add web-search tools here result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": query}]}) return result["messages"][-1].content
def _run_writer(request: str) -> str: agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools=[]) result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": request}]}) return result["messages"][-1].content
# --- expose workers as tools so the supervisor can call them ---
@tool def transfer_to_researcher(query: str) -> str: """Research a topic and return a summary of findings.""" return _run_researcher(query)
@tool def transfer_to_writer(request: str) -> str: """Draft or refine a piece of text given the request.""" return _run_writer(request)
# --- supervisor: a react agent that calls the worker tools ---
supervisor = create_react_agent( llm, tools=[transfer_to_researcher, transfer_to_writer], )
# --- run it --- result = supervisor.invoke( { "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Research the pros and cons of vector DBs vs graph DBs for RAG, then write a two-paragraph comparison." }] }, config={"recursion_limit": 20}, ) print(result["messages"][-1].content) ```
**Patterns that help in practice:**
- **Narrow tool docstrings** drive good delegation — the supervisor reads the docstring to decide which tool to call, so "Research a topic and return findings" outperforms "call researcher" - **Add a `FINISH` tool** that returns the final answer, so the supervisor can signal completion explicitly rather than relying on `END` propagation - **Parallel workers** require a different topology — if your workers can run concurrently, look at `langgraph-swarm` (fan-out/fan-in) rather than serial tool-call delegation - **State isolation is a feature** — each `create_react_agent` call gets a fresh `MessagesState`; if a worker needs shared context (a database schema, a user profile), pass it explicitly in the tool argument string
**Sources:** [LangGraph multi-agent supervisor tutorial](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/tutorials/multi_agent/agent_supervisor/) · [LangGraph prebuilt reference](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/prebuilt/)

item.title: Every Fine-Tuning Walkthrough Opens With `load_dataset('tatsu-lab/alpaca')` — Format Your Own Pairs as Alpaca or Messages JSONL and Push Them to the Hub in Three Steps
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Your QLoRA or SFT run assumes training data you never built. Format your instruction pairs as Alpaca or messages JSONL and push them to the Hub in three steps for any trainer.
item.content:encoded:
**Every fine-tuning walkthrough opens with someone else's dataset. Format your own instruction pairs and push them to the HuggingFace Hub in three steps so any trainer can use them.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Convert your own (instruction, response) pairs into a training dataset in either Alpaca or messages format, and publish it to the Hub so SFTTrainer, Unsloth, and torchtune can `load_dataset()` it from anywhere.
- Two formats cover almost all cases: flat **Alpaca** (`instruction`/`input`/`output`) for single-turn tasks like classification or summarization; a **messages array** (user/assistant turns) for conversational instruction-following — SFTTrainer, torchtune, and Unsloth all accept both - Quality beats volume: per the machinelearningplus dataset curation guide, 1,000 carefully curated examples consistently outperform 50,000 noisy ones; inconsistent formatting teaches the model inconsistent behavior - `dataset.push_to_hub("username/dataset-name")` publishes in one authenticated call; the dataset then loads identically from any Colab, VM, or CI training job
**Walk-through:**
```python import json from datasets import load_dataset
# 1. Build records — messages format for instruction-following models records = [ { "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this support ticket in one sentence."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "The user cannot reset their password via email."} ] }, # repeat for each instruction/response pair ]
# 2. Write to JSONL with open("train.jsonl", "w") as f: for r in records: f.write(json.dumps(r) + "\n")
# 3. Load and publish ds = load_dataset("json", data_files="train.jsonl", split="train") ds.push_to_hub("your-username/my-instruction-dataset", private=True)
# In any training script afterwards: # dataset = load_dataset("your-username/my-instruction-dataset", split="train") ```
For single-turn tasks with no conversational context, Alpaca format is simpler:
```json {"instruction": "Translate to French:", "input": "Hello, how are you?", "output": "Bonjour, comment allez-vous ?"} ```
SFTTrainer accepts Alpaca records via a `formatting_func`; the Hub auto-renders a dataset preview for both formats after the push.
**Limit:** For datasets over a few GB, add `max_shard_size="500MB"` to split into shards — the Hub uses Git LFS and single-file upload limits apply. More critically: vague instructions ("write code for X") produce vague model responses. Fix the lowest-quality 10% of your examples before adding more volume.
**Sources:** [HuggingFace Datasets — Share a dataset to the Hub](https://huggingface.co/docs/datasets/share) · [HuggingFace Hub LLM dataset upload guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/datasets-upload-guide-llm) · [machinelearningplus — Build instruction datasets for LLM fine-tuning](https://machinelearningplus.com/?p=35309)

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Loads the Same 800 Lines Into Every Turn — The @import Syntax Splits It Into Subdirectory Files That Only Load When Claude Enters That Path
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: A monolithic CLAUDE.md loads every line into every turn — the @import syntax splits it into subdirectory files that load only when Claude enters that path.
item.content:encoded:
**A monolithic CLAUDE.md loads every line into every turn — the `@path/to/file` import syntax splits it into subdirectory files that load only when Claude enters that path.**
Claude Code reads every loaded CLAUDE.md at the start of every session. A 600-line file that mixes your testing conventions, API patterns, and front-end component rules loads even when you are working on the database layer. The `@import` syntax lets you break that apart.
**How it works:**
In any CLAUDE.md, `@relative/path/to/file.md` expands that file inline at load time. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load automatically when Claude is working in that subtree — and nowhere else.
``` # CLAUDE.md (root — keep under ~80 lines) See architecture overview: @docs/claude/architecture.md Testing conventions: @docs/claude/testing.md ```
``` # app/CLAUDE.md (loads only when Claude is in app/) @app/docs/component-conventions.md Use RTL for component tests, not Playwright. ```
``` # worker/CLAUDE.md (loads only when Claude is in worker/) @worker/docs/edge-runtime-constraints.md No Node.js-only APIs in this directory. ```
When Claude is in `app/`, it reads the root CLAUDE.md plus `app/CLAUDE.md`. When it is in `worker/`, it reads the root plus `worker/CLAUDE.md`. Rules for a subsystem never pollute another subsystem's session.
**Setup steps:** 1. Run `/init` to generate a starting root CLAUDE.md from your codebase. 2. Identify your largest sections (architecture, testing, API patterns) and move each into a dedicated file under `docs/claude/`. 3. Replace those sections in the root with `@docs/claude/section.md` references. 4. Add per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md files for context that only applies in that tree. 5. Run `/context` to verify which files actually loaded in the current session.
**Limits:** `@import` is an inline expansion at load time, not lazy loading — imported content still counts toward your context window. The benefit is *scoping* (directory-specific rules stay out of unrelated sessions), not compression. Recursion depth is capped at five hops; a circular import fails silently without an error message.
**Sources:** [Claude Code memory docs — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) · [CLAUDE.md import patterns — morphllm.com](https://morphllm.com/claude-md-examples) · [Modular CLAUDE.md hierarchy guide — thepromptshelf.dev](https://thepromptshelf.dev/blog/claude-code-claude-md-too-long-hierarchy-guide-2026)

item.title: Your LangGraph Agent Runs Risky Tool Calls Without Asking — `interrupt()` Pauses the Graph, Saves State, and Resumes After the Human Responds
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: LangGraph's interrupt() halts any node mid-execution, persists state via a checkpointer, and resumes when you call Command(resume=value) — gate only the tool calls you can't undo.
item.content:encoded:
**LangGraph's `interrupt()` halts any node mid-execution, persists state via a checkpointer, and resumes when you call `Command(resume=value)` — gate only the tool calls you can't undo.**
An autonomous agent that can read files, write code, and call APIs will eventually need a pause before it does something irreversible — push to main, delete a database record, send an email. LangGraph's `interrupt()` handles this: it serializes the full graph state, returns control to your application, and continues from the exact same point once you supply a decision.
**Minimal working example:** ```python from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
def call_tool_node(state): action = state["messages"][-1].tool_calls[0] if action["name"] == "write_production_db": decision = interrupt({"action": action, "risk": "production write"}) if decision != "approve": return {"messages": [{"role": "tool", "content": "Cancelled by reviewer", "tool_call_id": action["id"]}]} # ... execute the tool ... return {...}
builder = StateGraph(MessagesState) builder.add_node("call_tool", call_tool_node) # ... add remaining nodes and edges ... graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())
# First run — pauses at interrupt() config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "my-task"}} result = graph.invoke({"messages": [...]}, config=config) # result["__interrupt__"] describes what was paused and why
# Human reviews, then resumes final = graph.invoke(Command(resume="approve"), config=config) ```
**Three things that trip people up:**
1. **The checkpointer is required.** `interrupt()` serializes state to the checkpoint store. Without `MemorySaver` (dev) or `PostgresSaver` (prod), `Command(resume=)` has nothing to resume from and the graph restarts from scratch.
2. **Reuse the exact same `thread_id` on resume.** A different thread id begins a new graph run, not a continuation of the interrupted one.
3. **Gate only the calls you can't undo.** Interrupting every tool call turns a useful automation into an approval queue. Identify the truly destructive actions (writes, sends, deletes) and let reads and lookups pass unblocked.
**What you can't do:** `interrupt()` inside a parallel fan-out (multiple concurrent edges) is currently unsupported — you'd need to gate before the fan-out, not inside it.
**Sources:** [Interrupts and Commands in LangGraph — DEV Community](https://dev.to/jamesbmour/interrupts-and-commands-in-langgraph-building-human-in-the-loop-workflows-4ngl) · [Building a human-in-the-loop approval gate — Machine Learning Mastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/building-a-human-in-the-loop-approval-gate-for-autonomous-agents/) · [Human-in-the-Loop Patterns — LangGraph docs](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/human_in_the_loop/)

item.title: Your RAG Pipeline Has No Objective Quality Signal — RAGAS Scores Context Recall, Faithfulness, and Precision in One Call and Points to Whether Your Retriever or Generator Is the Problem
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: RAGAS scores your RAG pipeline on four metrics using an LLM judge — and the combination of scores points directly to whether your retriever or generator is the problem.
item.content:encoded:
**RAGAS scores your RAG pipeline on four metrics in one call — and the combination tells you whether a low score is your retriever's problem or your generator's.**
After building a RAG pipeline, "it seems to work" is the only quality signal you have until users complain. RAGAS fixes that with four metrics, each measured by an LLM judge against your retrieved context and final answer:
| Metric | What it measures | Ground truth needed? | |---|---|---| | **Context recall** | Did the retriever return enough of what the question needed? | Yes | | **Context precision** | Did the retrieved chunks stay on-topic, or did noise get through? | No | | **Faithfulness** | Does the answer stick to the retrieved context, or is the model adding unsupported claims? | No | | **Answer relevancy** | Does the answer actually address the question? | No |
**Why all four matter together.** High precision + low faithfulness → your retriever is fine, your generator is hallucinating. Low context recall → the evidence never arrived, so the answer can't be correct regardless of the generator. The combination directs the fix.
**Install and run:** ```bash pip install ragas langchain-anthropic ```
```python from ragas import evaluate, EvaluationDataset, SingleTurnSample from ragas.metrics import LLMContextRecall, Faithfulness, LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from ragas.llms import LangchainLLMWrapper
judge = LangchainLLMWrapper(ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-5"))
samples = [ SingleTurnSample( user_input="What storage does Chroma use by default?", retrieved_contexts=[ "Chroma uses in-memory storage by default. " "Pass a path to PersistentClient to keep data on disk." ], response="Chroma stores data in memory by default.", reference="Chroma uses in-memory storage by default.", # needed for LLMContextRecall ), ] dataset = EvaluationDataset(samples=samples) result = evaluate( dataset, metrics=[LLMContextRecall(), Faithfulness(), LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference()], llm=judge, ) print(result) # {'context_recall': 1.0, 'faithfulness': 1.0, 'context_precision': 1.0} ```
Build your eval set from real user queries where you know the correct answer. Run it after every retrieval change — chunk size, embedding model, reranker threshold — to catch regressions before users do.
**The costs.** Context recall makes one judge call per sample; faithfulness makes two. A 100-sample eval set costs 300 LLM API calls. Price the eval set before committing to a judge model choice. The more critical limit: **hold the judge model and version fixed across every run you compare.** Swapping the judge changes the scores — not the pipeline — and the numbers become meaningless across runs.
**What RAGAS can't catch:** whether your chunking strategy preserves enough context (that's a pre-retrieval problem), and whether the ground-truth references you wrote are actually correct (garbage in, garbage out).
**Sources:** [Evaluate a simple RAG system — docs.ragas.io](https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/getstarted/rag_eval/) · [RAG Evaluation with RAGAS — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/rag-evaluation-with-ragas) · [Ragas: how to measure your RAG pipeline — DEV Community](https://dev.to/m_t_ramkrushna/ragas-how-to-actually-measure-your-rag-pipeline-faithfulness-context-precisionrecall-relevancy-26)

item.title: You Download GGUF Weights From Someone Else's Compression Run Because Converting Your Own Looks Complicated — Two llama.cpp Commands Turn Any HuggingFace Checkpoint Into Q4_K_M in 20 Minutes
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Convert any HuggingFace checkpoint to a 4-bit GGUF for local use: convert_hf_to_gguf.py → llama-quantize Q4_K_M → Ollama. Three commands, no GPU needed for the quantization step.
item.content:encoded:
**You download GGUF weights from someone else's compression run because converting a model yourself looks complicated — `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` and `llama-quantize` do it in three commands.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Convert any HuggingFace model checkpoint — including your own fine-tuned ones — to a 4-bit GGUF file, then run it with Ollama or llama-server without waiting for someone else to cut a release.
**Three things worth knowing before you start:**
1. **Q4_K_M is the right default.** The K-quant series uses per-block scale factors, averaging ~4.5 bits/weight rather than a hard 4 bits. Compared to legacy Q4_0, it scores measurably better on benchmarks at the same file size. Q8_0 halves full-precision size with nearly lossless quality but doubles Q4_K_M's file size — save it for models you're actively evaluating, not deploying.
2. **Budget 3–4× the target model's final GGUF size in temporary disk space.** The pipeline keeps the original weights, an F16 intermediate, and the final GGUF on disk at the same time. For a 7B model the F16 intermediate alone is ~14 GB.
3. **Conversion needs no GPU.** `llama-quantize` runs on CPU and finishes in 5–15 minutes for a 7B model. You only need a GPU if you want to run inference afterward.
**The recipe (Qwen2.5-3B as example — works for any supported architecture):**
```bash # 1. Build llama.cpp git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc)
# 2. Download from HuggingFace pip install huggingface_hub huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct --local-dir ../Qwen2.5-3B
# 3. Convert to F16 GGUF (keep this — re-quantize to other formats without re-downloading) python3 convert_hf_to_gguf.py ../Qwen2.5-3B --outfile ../Qwen2.5-3B-f16.gguf --outtype f16
# 4. Quantize to Q4_K_M ./build/bin/llama-quantize ../Qwen2.5-3B-f16.gguf ../Qwen2.5-3B-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M
# 5a. Run directly ./build/bin/llama-cli -m ../Qwen2.5-3B-Q4_K_M.gguf -p "Hello" -n 128
# 5b. Register with Ollama and run via its API printf 'FROM ../Qwen2.5-3B-Q4_K_M.gguf ' > Modelfile ollama create qwen2.5-3b-q4 -f Modelfile && ollama run qwen2.5-3b-q4 ```
**The limit that matters:** `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` handles most transformer architectures, but Mixture-of-Experts models (Mixtral, DeepSeek-MoE) need `--split-max-tensors` and convert more slowly. Check the [llama.cpp issues](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues) for your architecture before starting a large download. If conversion errors with "type not supported", try `--outtype bf16` first. Quantization degrades reasoning tasks more than factual recall — test on your actual workload before switching a production pipeline.
**Sources:** [llama.cpp quantize README](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/quantize/README.md) · [llama.cpp imatrix README](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/imatrix/README.md) · [Quantizing LLMs with llama.cpp — practitioner walk-through](https://medium.com/@dogucuburak/quantizing-llms-with-llama-cpp-6eb9f48d1819)

item.title: Claude Code Works Through Long Tasks Without Volunteering What It Noticed Along the Way — `cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin` Adds a Side Agent That Flags Those Observations
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: A built-in, off-by-default Claude Code mod adds a background side agent that surfaces missed observations above your prompt during long sessions — one command to enable, no configuration needed.
item.content:encoded:
**A built-in Claude Code mod adds a background side agent that flags observations you might have missed — things it noticed but wasn't asked about. One command to enable, no configuration.**
Claude Code doesn't interrupt a running task to surface a concern it noticed while doing something else. If it spots a constraint conflict or a pattern that may cause trouble later, it typically finishes what it was asked and moves on — you get the result but not the flag.
`cc-plugin-you-should-know` is a built-in mod that adds a background side agent to every session. While Claude works on a long task, the side agent rereads the conversation and posts a note above your prompt when it finds something worth flagging — an instruction from earlier that the current approach may violate, an assumption that no longer holds, a pattern it noticed that wasn't the subject of any specific ask.
Enable it:
``` /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin ```
Disable it:
``` /plugin disable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin ```
Or manage from the Installed tab of `/plugin`.
**What it sees — and doesn't.** The side agent has no tools. No file reads, no shell access, no ability to affect what Claude does next. Its only input is the conversation thread. It catches things visible in that thread: a constraint you set at the start that a later step quietly ignored, an instruction your latest request contradicts, something you said you wanted that the current approach abandoned. For anything that requires reading the filesystem or running a command, it won't catch what hasn't been told to it.
**Real limits to know before you enable it.** On a long, dense session it runs a separate model request each turn — added latency and token cost proportional to your context length. The mod is off by default precisely for this reason. It's designed for interactive long sessions, not headless or CI runs where you want minimal overhead. Requires Claude Code v2.1.287+. Built-in mods are not blocked by `--safe-mode` or `disableAllHooks` — worth noting if you restrict third-party plugins for security, since this one cannot be turned off at the org level.
