item.title: Your Claude App Returns Text When the Question Needs a Live Lookup — Tool Use Gives Claude a Typed JSON Schema, Gets a `tool_use` Block Back, and Lets Your Code Handle the Rest
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Define a function with a JSON Schema, pass it as tools[], handle the tool_use response block, run your code, return a tool_result — Claude then finishes its answer. Every Claude-based agent uses this five-step loop.
item.content:encoded:
**Define a function with a JSON Schema, pass it as `tools[]`, check `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, run your function, send a `tool_result` — Claude finishes its answer. Five steps, every agent app uses this loop.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Wire any Python function into a Claude conversation so Claude calls it when a question needs live data or computation - Implement the full `tool_use` → `tool_result` round-trip without guessing about message format - Control call behavior: require a specific tool, require any tool, or let Claude decide with `tool_choice`
---
Claude's Messages API returns text by default. Tool use (function calling) adds a richer exchange: you describe functions with JSON Schema and pass them as `tools`. When Claude decides a function is needed, it returns a `tool_use` block instead of (or before) its text. Your code runs the function and sends back a `tool_result`. Claude uses that result to finish the answer.
Every Claude-based agent — whether it queries a database, calls an API, runs a shell command, or routes to another service — is built on this loop.
**Step 1 — Define a tool with a JSON Schema:**
```python tools = [{ "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather for a city", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "location": { "type": "string", "description": "City and state, e.g. 'Austin, TX'" }, "unit": {"type": "string", "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"]} }, "required": ["location"] } }] ```
**Step 2 — Make the first request with `tools` attached:**
```python import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() msg1 = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Austin right now?"}] ) ```
**Step 3 — Check whether Claude called a tool:**
```python if msg1.stop_reason == "tool_use": call = next(b for b in msg1.content if b.type == "tool_use") # call.name == "get_weather" # call.input == {"location": "Austin, TX"} # call.id == "toolu_01..." ```
**Step 4 — Run your function and send the result back:**
```python result = fetch_weather(call.input["location"], call.input.get("unit", "fahrenheit"))
msg2 = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Austin right now?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": msg1.content}, {"role": "user", "content": [{ "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id, "content": result }]} ] ) print(msg2.content[0].text) # "It's currently 72°F and partly cloudy in Austin." ```
**Controlling when Claude calls tools.** Default `tool_choice={"type": "auto"}` lets Claude decide. `{"type": "any"}` requires at least one call this turn. `{"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}` forces that specific function. `{"type": "none"}` passes tools for reference only — Claude won't call them.
**The limit that catches people first.** The example above handles one tool call per turn. A real task may need several — Claude calls a function, you return the result, it calls another. Loop until `msg.stop_reason == "end_turn"`. The SDK's `ToolRunner` (available in beta via `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) handles this loop automatically if you pass a Python callable alongside each tool definition, which removes the message-building bookkeeping entirely.
Add `strict: True` to the tool definition to get guaranteed schema-conformant inputs from Claude, preventing malformed calls from reaching your function at the cost of some extra prompt tokens.
**Sources:** [Tool use overview — docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use) · [Implement tool use — docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use)

item.title: Your LoRA Adapter Disappears When the Colab Session Closes — `model.push_to_hub()` Persists It to HuggingFace in Two Lines
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: PEFT's push_to_hub() uploads only the adapter weights — often under 50 MB — not the full base model. AutoPeftModel.from_pretrained() reconstructs the full model at load time from the adapter and the base model's Hub weights.
item.content:encoded:
**PEFT's `model.push_to_hub()` saves only the adapter weights — often under 50 MB instead of gigabytes — and `AutoPeftModel.from_pretrained()` reconstructs the full model at load time.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Persist a fine-tuned LoRA adapter from a Colab session to HuggingFace Hub so it survives the runtime closing - Share just the adapter (not the 7B base weights) with your team or load it in a different environment - Reload the full fine-tuned model in a single line from any machine that has Hub access
---
After a QLoRA training run, the trained adapter lives in memory (or in `/tmp`). The Colab session will eventually disconnect. The common mistake is to forget the upload step until after the runtime is gone.
**Path 1: Adapter-only upload (PEFT model object)**
```python from peft import AutoPeftModelForCausalLM
# model is your PeftModelForCausalLM (the object returned by get_peft_model or loaded via PEFT) model.push_to_hub("your-username/llama-3-lora-finetune") tokenizer.push_to_hub("your-username/llama-3-lora-finetune") ```
This uploads `adapter_config.json` and `adapter_model.safetensors` — typically 10–100 MB depending on `r` and `target_modules`. The base model weights stay on Hub under their original repo.
**Loading it back:**
```python from peft import AutoPeftModelForCausalLM
model = AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "your-username/llama-3-lora-finetune", torch_dtype="auto", device_map="auto", ) ```
PEFT resolves the base model automatically from `adapter_config.json`'s `base_model_name_or_path` field and downloads it from Hub if not cached.
**Path 2: Upload the merged model**
If you've already called `merge_and_unload()` (the full weights are in memory), push the merged model directly:
```python merged = model.merge_and_unload() merged.save_pretrained("./merged-model") # local fallback merged.push_to_hub("your-username/llama-3-finetuned-merged") tokenizer.push_to_hub("your-username/llama-3-finetuned-merged") ```
The merged upload is the full model size (7B ≈ 14 GB in bf16). Use Path 1 for sharing; use Path 2 when you want a self-contained deployment artifact.
**Limits to know:** - A Hub write token is required (`huggingface_hub.login(token="hf_...")` or `huggingface-cli login`). Hub tokens are scoped: a "read" token cannot push. - Private repos require a Pro account or an Organization with private model capacity. Public uploads are unlimited. - `adapter_config.json` records the original base model ID — if the recipient does not have that base model licensed (e.g. Llama 3 gated access), `AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained()` will fail on the base model download. Adapter-only sharing is not a license workaround. - Large merged models (>10 GB) benefit from `--lfs-migrate` chunking if you hit Git LFS push timeouts.
**Sources:** [PEFT quicktour — huggingface.co/docs/peft](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/main/en/quicktour), [Share a model — huggingface.co/docs/transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_sharing), [Fine-tune SmolLM on synthetic data (community walkthrough, David Berenstein) — huggingface.co/blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/davidberenstein1957/fine-tune-a-smollm-on-synthetic-data-of-llm) (end-to-end pipeline including the Hub push step)

item.title: Your Headless Claude Code Run Has Full Write Access When You Only Needed Read — `--allowedTools` Scopes the Tool Palette Before the First Call
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Pass --allowedTools Read,Glob,Bash to a headless Claude Code run and every unlisted tool fails immediately — no permission prompt, no silent file edit. Scoped entries like Bash(npm test:*) restrict individual commands.
item.content:encoded:
**Pass `--allowedTools Read,Glob,Bash` to any headless run and Claude Code rejects every unlisted tool call immediately — no permission prompt, no accidental file edit, no waiting on approval in CI.**
When you use Claude Code in headless mode (`-p` / `--print`), it has the same tool access as an interactive session by default. A CI analysis step, a code-review pass, or a documentation audit might call `Edit` or `Write` when you only wanted reads. In non-interactive mode there is no "ask" prompt — the action simply runs.
**The flag:**
```bash # Analysis only: Claude can read and run commands, but cannot write files claude --allowedTools "Read,Glob,Bash" \ --print "Find the three files with the most TODO comments and report them." ```
If Claude tries to call `Write` or `Edit`, the call fails immediately with a permission error that Claude sees as a tool result and can reason about (it will not retry silently).
**Scoped tool names** lock Claude down even further — each entry is `ToolName(allowed-prefix:*)`:
```bash # Can only run npm test and git log, nothing else in Bash claude --allowedTools "Read,Glob,Bash(npm test:*),Bash(git log:*)" \ --print "Run tests and summarise any new failures vs the last commit." ```
The prefix match is a prefix, not a glob — `Bash(npm:*)` allows `npm test`, `npm run build`, etc., but not `rm`.
**Common patterns:**
| Use case | `--allowedTools` value | |---|---| | Read-only audit / code review | `Read,Glob` | | Test runner + log reader | `Bash(npm test:*),Bash(jest:*),Read,Glob` | | Git analysis only | `Bash(git:*),Read,Glob` | | Full analysis, no writes | `Read,Glob,Bash` |
**Limits:** - Every tool the task needs must be explicitly listed. A missing tool fails the call; Claude reports the failure and may abort the task entirely rather than working around it. - `--allowedTools` is a whitelist, not a transformer — you cannot use it to redirect a tool call to a different tool. - Tool names are case-sensitive (`Read` not `read`; `Bash` not `bash`). - MCP tools are referenced by their server-prefixed names: `mcp__github__get_file_contents`, not `get_file_contents`.
**Sources:** [Headless mode reference — code.claude.com/docs/en/headless](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless), [Claude Code CLI flags — code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference), [OWASP LLM Top 10: LLM06 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm06-excessive-agency/) (the principle behind least-privilege tool grants)

item.title: Your Claude Code Agent Polls for Completion With Sleep Loops — Monitor Streams Every Background Process Line as a Live Event Instead
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: The Monitor tool runs a command and delivers each stdout line back as a separate notification — the agent reacts to test failures or deploy completions in real time instead of polling with sleep loops.
item.content:encoded:
**The Monitor tool feeds each stdout line from a background command back as a separate notification — the agent reacts to completions and failures without sleep loops, polling Bash calls, or missed intermediate output.**
When a Claude Code workflow kicks off a long-running task — a test suite, a deploy script, a server start — the common pattern is `Bash("sleep 10 && check-status.sh")`. It fires after an arbitrary wait, misses output emitted between checks, and costs a round-trip per poll. A missed failure message means the agent retries unnecessarily; an early check means it runs the command again before the first finishes.
**Monitor replaces polling with a direct event stream.** It runs a command and delivers each stdout line back as its own notification in the conversation transcript. The agent reads each line and decides: keep watching, stop the task, or trigger a follow-up.
```bash # Watch a test suite as it runs — react on each line Monitor("pnpm test --reporter=verbose 2>&1") # Notifications arrive live: # "✓ auth.spec.ts (5 tests passed)" # "✗ billing.spec.ts FAILED: timeout after 5000ms" # The agent calls TaskStop(task_id) the moment it sees the failure ```
**WebSocket sources** — for dev servers or event buses, pass a `ws://` URL and each incoming message becomes a notification:
```bash Monitor("ws://localhost:3000/events") ```
**Plugin monitors** — declare a background watcher in your plugin's manifest and it starts automatically when the plugin activates:
```json "monitors": [{"command": "node scripts/watch-ci.mjs", "label": "CI watch"}] ```
**Limits:** - Default timeout: 300 s. Configurable up to 1800 s; requests above that are capped at the maximum. - Monitors are session-scoped — background tasks and monitors do not carry over on session resume. - WebSocket watches require a separate permission approval from command watches. - **Oct 23, 2026:** Monitor now works when Claude Code is deployed through AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Azure Foundry — previously it was limited to direct API sessions and claude.ai/code.
Stop an active monitor with `TaskStop(task_id)` once the agent has seen what it needs.
**Sources:** [Tools reference — code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference) · [Changelog Oct 23 — code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog)

item.title: Your Local Model Dev Loop Has No HTTP Endpoint — `llama-server` Turns Any GGUF Into a Local OpenAI-Compatible API in One Command
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Run `llama-server -m model.gguf` and get a localhost:8080 OpenAI-compatible endpoint — point your existing openai Python client at it with base_url changed and no API key needed.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `llama-server -m model.gguf --port 8080` and your existing OpenAI client works against a local model by changing `base_url` to `http://localhost:8080/v1` and setting `api_key="none"`.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run any GGUF-format quantized model as a local HTTP server, iterate on prompts and tool-calling without API credit meters or internet access, and reuse your existing `openai` Python client unchanged — except for one parameter.
## Install and start the server
```bash # macOS brew install llama.cpp
# Ubuntu — build from source git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc) cp build/bin/llama-server /usr/local/bin/
# Download a quantized GGUF from HuggingFace huggingface-cli download bartowski/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GGUF --include "Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf" --local-dir ./models
# Start the server llama-server -m ./models/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --ctx-size 8192 --n-gpu-layers 99 # push all layers to VRAM; 0 = CPU-only ```
## Point your OpenAI client at it
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( base_url="http://localhost:8080/v1", api_key="none" # llama-server accepts any non-empty string )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="any", # server ignores this — uses the loaded model messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG in one sentence."}] ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
The server also accepts tool definitions and returns structured outputs — useful for testing your agent's tool-calling logic locally before sending to a hosted model.
## Three flags that matter
| Flag | Default | What to change | |---|---|---| | `--ctx-size` | 4096 | Match your actual use case; larger needs more VRAM/RAM | | `--n-gpu-layers` | 0 (CPU) | `-ngl 99` to push all layers to GPU | | `--parallel` | 1 | Set `--parallel 4` if your code makes concurrent requests |
## Limits vs Ollama
llama.cpp server is more direct but less managed than Ollama: you download and reference GGUF files manually, there is no model registry or pull command, and single-threaded generation queues requests unless you set `--parallel`. Ollama is easier for day-to-day use; llama.cpp server is better when you want finer control over context size, GPU offload layers, or you're scripting server startup in CI.
RAM budget: Q4_K_M on an 8 B model needs ~5 GB; a 70 B model at Q4 needs ~40 GB. Do not expose `--host 0.0.0.0` on an untrusted network — there is no built-in authentication.
**Sources:** [llama.cpp REST API reference — ggml.ai](https://www.mintlify.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/api/rest/overview) · [Starting with llama.cpp — Open WebUI docs](https://docs.openwebui.com/getting-started/quick-start/starting-with-llama-cpp) · [llama-server tutorial — Arm Learning Path](https://learn.arm.com/learning-paths/servers-and-cloud-computing/llama-cpu/llama-server)

item.title: Your Subagent Starts Fresh Every Session — Add `memory: project` to Its Frontmatter and Claude Code Creates a Persistent Memory Directory
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Add `memory: project` to your .claude/agents frontmatter and the subagent gets a persistent directory — MEMORY.md loads (200 lines or 25 KB) into its context on the next session.
item.content:encoded:
**Add `memory: project` to a `.claude/agents/*.md` file and Claude Code creates `.claude/agent-memory/<name>/` — the subagent can write what it learns to `MEMORY.md` there, and the first 200 lines (or 25 KB) load back into its context next session.**
A Claude Code subagent's context resets with every new session. If your reviewer agent discovered last week that the helpers in `tests/utils.py` are deprecated, it will discover them again Monday — because there is no connection between sessions unless you explicitly create one.
The `memory` frontmatter field creates that connection:
```yaml --- name: code-reviewer description: Review changed code for correctness and style issues memory: project --- ```
With `memory: project`, Claude Code creates `.claude/agent-memory/code-reviewer/` and injects that path into the subagent's system prompt. The subagent can write a `MEMORY.md` there — conventions to enforce, patterns that have gone wrong, team norms it has inferred — and the first 200 lines (or 25 KB, whichever comes first) load into its context automatically on the next session.
**Three scope choices:**
| Scope | Path | Use for | |---|---|---| | `user` | `~/.claude/agent-memory/<name>/` | Personal agents used across projects | | `project` | `.claude/agent-memory/<name>/` | Shared team knowledge — commit it | | `local` | `.claude/agent-memory-local/<name>/` | Project knowledge that stays gitignored |
`project` is the recommended default. Commit `.claude/agent-memory/` and the whole team starts each session with what the subagent has learned.
**Two gotchas:** 1. If auto memory is disabled (`autoMemoryEnabled: false` or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`), the `memory` field has no effect. 2. A write that pushes `MEMORY.md` past the 200-line read limit now throws an explicit error instead of silently truncating — prune old entries when it gets long.
Requires Claude Code v2.1.277 or later.
**Sources:** [Create custom subagents — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) · [How Claude remembers your project — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)

item.title: Your LangGraph Agent Forgets Everything When the Process Restarts — Three Lines Replace MemorySaver With a Persistent Backend
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: LangGraph has three checkpointer backends: MemorySaver (dev only), SqliteSaver (local file), and PostgresSaver (production). Swapping them is one line; thread_id scopes state to a conversation.
item.content:encoded:
**LangGraph has three checkpointer backends: MemorySaver for dev, SqliteSaver for local persistence, PostgresSaver for production. Swapping them is one line; `thread_id` in each call scopes state to a conversation.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Make any LangGraph agent's state survive process restarts — resume interrupted conversations, serve multiple users with separate state, and recover from failures at the last successful checkpoint.
**The three-tier progression:**
```python from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver # built-in from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver # pip install langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver # pip install langgraph-checkpoint-postgres psycopg[binary]
# Development / testing — in-process only, lost on restart checkpointer = MemorySaver()
# Local development — file-backed, single process, persists across restarts checkpointer = SqliteSaver.from_conn_string("checkpoints.db")
# Production — survives restarts, safe for multi-process deploys checkpointer = PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) checkpointer.setup() # run once per new database; creates the required tables and indexes ```
Wire the checkpointer into the compiled graph:
```python graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer) ```
Every invocation scopes its state to a `thread_id`:
```python result = graph.invoke( {"messages": [HumanMessage(content=user_input)]}, config={"configurable": {"thread_id": session_id}} ) ```
Different `thread_id`s get separate histories. The same one picks up where the last call left off — including across process restarts with SqliteSaver or PostgresSaver.
**Three gotchas before you deploy:**
1. **`checkpointer.setup()` is required once.** It creates the tables and indexes PostgresSaver needs. The official examples have it commented out — run it on any new database, or writes will silently fail. 2. **Raw `psycopg` connections need two options.** If you pass a raw connection instead of using `from_conn_string()`, set `autocommit=True` and `row_factory=dict_row` — without them, operations can raise a `TypeError`. 3. **No built-in checkpoint retention.** Thread histories accumulate indefinitely. Add a cleanup job that prunes checkpoints older than a threshold, or the database grows without bound.
For async agents: use `AsyncPostgresSaver` from `langgraph.checkpoint.postgres.aio` and `AsyncSqliteSaver` from `langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite.aio` — same API, async context managers.
**Sources:** [LangGraph Persistence — LangChain Docs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) · [How to add memory — LangChain Docs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory) · [LangChain Support: checkpointer patterns](https://support.langchain.com/articles/6253531756-understanding-checkpointers-databases-api-memory-and-ttl)

item.title: Your Parallel Subagents Edit the Same Files and Undo Each Other's Work — Add `isolation: worktree` to Their Frontmatter
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Set isolation: worktree in .claude/agents/<name>.md frontmatter to give each subagent a private git checkout; parallel sessions write separate file trees and can't overwrite each other.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `isolation: worktree` in `.claude/agents/<name>.md` to give each subagent invocation a private git checkout; parallel sessions write to separate file trees and can't overwrite each other.**
When two or more subagents run on the same repo at the same time, they share the same working tree. One agent's file changes overwrite another's — whichever runs second wins, silently discarding the first agent's edits. The problem scales with how many files your subagents touch.
The fix is one frontmatter field. Open `.claude/agents/<name>.md` and add:
```yaml --- name: refactorer description: Refactors a module in isolation isolation: worktree --- ```
Claude Code provisions each invocation in its own git worktree: a separate checkout branched from your default branch. The two sessions see different file trees and cannot collide.
**Three things to know:**
1. **Base branch defaults to your repo's default branch.** If you need the subagent to see your local uncommitted changes, set `worktree.baseRef: "head"` in your session settings. Without it, the worktree branches from origin/main (or equivalent), so any unmerged local edits are invisible to it.
2. **Agent teams don't use worktrees.** The experimental agent teams feature doesn't isolate teammates in worktrees — partition the work so each teammate owns a different set of files instead.
3. **Cleanup is automatic.** A worktree with no changes is removed when the subagent exits. One with changes stays on disk until a periodic sweep can remove it without losing work; you don't need to clean up manually.
You can also ask Claude verbally — "use worktrees for your agents" — without editing any frontmatter. The frontmatter version persists the behavior for every future invocation of that agent.

item.title: Your Vector Store Returns the Documents That Mention Your Query — A Cross-Encoder Scores Pairs to Find the Ones That Actually Answer It
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Two-stage RAG: vector search retrieves the top 20-50 candidates, then a CrossEncoder scores each (query, doc) pair to surface the 5-10 that truly answer the query.
item.content:encoded:
**Two-stage RAG: fast vector search retrieves 20–50 candidates, then a cross-encoder scores each (query, document) pair to surface the 5–10 that genuinely answer the query.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** take the candidates your vector store returns, rerank them against the query using a cross-encoder, and cut the noise before the LLM ever sees the context.
**Three things to take away:**
- A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently — fast for full-corpus search, but blind to the relationship between them. A cross-encoder sees both together, so it scores true relevance rather than vector proximity. - The two-stage pipeline resolves the tradeoff: vector search for recall (retrieve top 20–50), cross-encoder for precision (rerank to top 5–10), then generate. - Every query runs the full model over each candidate pair with no caching between queries. At N=50 on CPU, expect 200–500ms of reranking latency on top of retrieval — keep stage-1 N small and use batching for production.
**Running it with sentence-transformers:**
```python from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
model = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")
# candidates: list of strings from your vector store's top-N results pairs = [(query, doc) for doc in candidates] scores = model.predict(pairs) # shape: (len(candidates),)
ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates), reverse=True) top_k = [doc for _, doc in ranked[:5]] ```
`cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` is the standard English starting point (~22M parameters, fast for small batches). For multilingual use or higher accuracy, `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` is the common upgrade — it supports multiple languages but runs slower per pair.
**What it costs you:** the CrossEncoder has no vector index — it runs inference on every (query, doc) pair on each request. There is no pre-computation shortcut. For N > a few hundred, the latency becomes the bottleneck; batch-process pairs and run on GPU to stay practical.
**Anchor resource:** [Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking — Advanced Retrieval for AI with Chroma, DeepLearning.AI (free, ~1h)](https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/advanced-retrieval-for-ai/lesson/5/cross-encoder-re-ranking) — lesson 5 builds the two-stage retriever end to end in a runnable notebook.
**Sources:** [Advanced Retrieval for AI — DeepLearning.AI](https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/advanced-retrieval-for-ai) · [CrossEncoder reranker — LangChain docs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/document_transformers/cross_encoder_reranker) · [cross-encoder models — Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/cross-encoder) · [RAG Complete Tutorial Part 4: Reranking — GopenAI](https://blog.gopenai.com/rag-complete-tutorial-part-04-f89f5c076744)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Doesn't Show You Which Permission Rules Are Firing — `claude_code.safety_event` Puts Every Block Into Your OTel Trace
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: claude_code.safety_event (Oct 21 changelog) fires on every tool call a permission rule, hook, auto mode, or sandbox blocks or prompts — attributes include category, rule_source, grant_scope, and circuit_breaker.
item.content:encoded:
**Every tool call Claude Code blocks or prompts now emits a `claude_code.safety_event` OpenTelemetry span — the Oct 21 changelog addition that closes the governance gap between "we have rules" and "we know what they're doing."**
Without this, a team deploying Claude Code through Bedrock or Vertex with a managed settings file had no visibility into which rules were actually triggering — or whether auto mode's classifier was being too conservative. They saw Claude stop or ask; they did not see what stopped it.
The new span fires on every blocked or prompted tool call and carries four key attributes:
- **`category`**: `permission_rule` (a deny/ask rule outside managed settings), `managed_policy` (from managed settings), `auto_mode` (the classifier decided), `hook` (a hook returned an error or deny), or `sandbox` (sandboxing blocked the call) - **`rule_source`**: which settings file the triggering rule came from — useful when rules merge from user, project, and managed layers - **`grant_scope`**: for prompted calls, whether the user approved once or for the full session - **`circuit_breaker`**: for built-in safety checks, the check name — `dangerousRemoval`, `outsideReadsBlocked`, `claudeSettingsFile`, etc.
**Correlating to the tool call**: match the `tool_use_id` on the safety event to the `claude_code.tool_decision` span for that call. `tool_decision` now also carries `classifier_verdict` and `permission_mode`, so you can distinguish auto mode blocks from explicit rules.
**Three practical uses:**
1. **Governance audit**: count events by `category` and `rule_source` over a day. If `managed_policy` events are sparse, your org-level rules may not be covering what people actually do. 2. **Auto mode tuning**: if `auto_mode` events dominate your blocked calls, the classifier is blocking more than your explicit rules do. Check `classifier_category` (requires `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` to include) to see what the classifier named. 3. **Per-session debugging**: a developer whose session is unusually slow can look for unexpected `hook` or `permission_rule` events in the trace waterfall.
**Limits**: Not every refused call emits a safety event — calls rejected before a `tool_use_id` is assigned have none. The standard OTEL exporter environment variables are ignored in repo-scoped settings files; configure them in managed or personal settings instead. And `classifier_category` is redacted by default; `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` exposes it, but also logs more sensitive decision context, so enable it deliberately.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog — Oct 21 `claude_code.safety_event` entry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Monitoring and observability docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) · [Observability with OpenTelemetry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/observability)

item.title: vLLM v0.32.0 Raises the Floor to Python 3.11 and Locks Down CORS Origins — Check These Three Breaking Changes Before Upgrading
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: vLLM v0.32.0 (Oct 18, 814 commits) drops Python 3.10, restricts default CORS to same-origin, and removes cascade attention — three things to audit before running pip install --upgrade vllm.
item.content:encoded:
**vLLM v0.32.0 shipped October 18 with 814 commits from 363 contributors. Three of them break existing deployments without an obvious error at startup.**
**Python 3.11 minimum.** Python 3.10 support is dropped. If your container image pins `python:3.10` — or inherits it from a base image — the package install may succeed but C-extension bindings will likely crash at import time. Audit your Dockerfile before upgrading the package.
**Default CORS restricted to same-origin.** vLLM's built-in HTTP server previously accepted cross-origin requests by default. v0.32.0 tightens the default to same-origin only. If your frontend or API gateway calls the vLLM endpoint from a different origin and relied on the open default, add `--allowed-origins "*"` (or your specific origins) explicitly to the serve command.
**Cascade attention removed.** The `--use-cascade-attention` flag still parses without error in v0.32.0 — it is silently a no-op. The flag is scheduled for full removal in v0.33.0. Remove it from start scripts now to avoid a hard error on the next upgrade.
**Why it matters:** Python 3.11 is required for the next generation of vLLM's C extensions; projects still on 3.10 need a base-image update before the package upgrade.
**Sources:** [vLLM v0.32.0 release notes](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.32.0)

item.title: Your Embedding Search Scans Every Vector on Every Query — FAISS's Two-Index Trade-off Cuts That to a Fixed Cluster Search
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: IndexFlatL2 gives exact nearest-neighbor search with zero training; IndexIVFFlat partitions vectors into cells and searches only nprobe of them — trade a fraction of recall for speed.
item.content:encoded:
**FAISS's two indexes trade recall for speed: IndexFlatL2 scans every vector (exact, no training); IndexIVFFlat partitions into cells and searches nprobe of them (approximate, fast).**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Build an in-memory vector similarity index with FAISS — from exact search for small collections to cell-partitioned approximate search for millions of vectors — and understand the one parameter (`nprobe`) that controls the recall/speed trade-off.
- **IndexFlatL2** computes distance from the query to every vector in the index. Recall is always 100%; cost scales linearly with collection size. Correct choice up to ~100k vectors. - **IndexIVFFlat** partitions the space into `nlist` Voronoi cells at training time and assigns each vector to its nearest cell. At query time it searches only the nearest `nprobe` cells. Typical result at `nprobe=10` with `nlist=256`: 95–99% recall at a fraction of the brute-force cost. - **The `nprobe` dial**: higher = more recall, more compute. Start with `nprobe=10` and benchmark against a ground-truth set before setting a production value.
**Walk-through:**
```python import faiss import numpy as np
# 50,000 embeddings at 768 dimensions (e.g. from sentence-transformers) d = 768 n = 50_000 rng = np.random.default_rng(42) vecs = rng.random((n, d)).astype("float32") # FAISS requires float32
# ── Exact search (IndexFlatL2) ────────────────────────────────────────────── flat = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) flat.add(vecs) # no training required D, I = flat.search(vecs[:5], k=3) # top-3 nearest neighbors
# ── Approximate search (IndexIVFFlat) ────────────────────────────────────── nlist = 256 # cells; rule of thumb: sqrt(n) to 4*sqrt(n) quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) # coarse quantizer assigns vectors to cells ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, nlist, faiss.METRIC_L2)
assert not ivf.is_trained ivf.train(vecs) # required: learns cell centroids from data ivf.add(vecs)
ivf.nprobe = 10 # search 10 of 256 cells; tune for recall D_ivf, I_ivf = ivf.search(vecs[:5], k=3)
# ── Save / reload ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── faiss.write_index(ivf, "index.faiss") loaded = faiss.read_index("index.faiss") ```
**When FAISS fits:** FAISS is pure in-process RAM — no server, no HTTP calls, no schema. It is the right tool for a prototype, a batch pipeline that rebuilds the index on every run, or a service where the full vector set fits in memory. Once the collection grows past available RAM, you need live updates, or you need metadata filtering (e.g. "only documents tagged topic:rag"), reach for Qdrant, Chroma, or pgvector instead — each of which was covered in earlier posts in this series.
Install: `pip install faiss-cpu` (CPU-only); `faiss-gpu` for GPU acceleration on CUDA hardware.
**Sources:** [FAISS Getting Started](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Getting-started), [PyImageSearch: Vector Search with FAISS — ANN Explained](https://pyimagesearch.com/2026/02/16/vector-search-with-faiss-approximate-nearest-neighbor-ann-explained/), [Pinecone FAISS Tutorial](https://pinecone.io/learn/faiss-tutorial)

item.title: Your Claude Code Monitor Commands Were Silently No-Ops on Bedrock and Vertex — v2.1.307 Fixes That and Brings Cross-Session Messaging to Enterprise Deployments
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.307 (Oct 23) enables Monitor, SendMessage, and ListAgents on Bedrock, Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry — Monitor was silently inoperable on these backends until now.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code v2.1.307 (Oct 23) enables Monitor, plugin monitors, SendMessage, and ListAgents on Bedrock, Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry — Monitor was previously silently inoperable on these backends.**
If your organization routes Claude Code through AWS Bedrock or Google Vertex (as most enterprise deployments do), Monitor calls were accepted without error but doing nothing. The same was true in sessions where nonessential traffic is disabled. As of Oct 23, all behaviors match the direct Anthropic API.
**What Monitor actually does:** it runs a command in the background and feeds each line of output back to Claude as the command runs — not after it finishes. Claude Code invokes it as a first-class tool call during a session:
``` Monitor(command="pytest --tb=short -q", timeout=120) # Claude sees each test result as it streams; it can start fixing failures # before the full suite finishes, rather than reading the dump at the end ```
A Claude Code session watching `pytest` in real time can iterate on failures inline rather than running the full suite, reading output, then fixing — cutting the outer loop from minutes to seconds on large test suites.
**Cross-session messaging on enterprise backends:** `SendMessage` (send a message to a named running session) and `ListAgents` (enumerate active sessions) also work now on Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry. Multi-agent workflows that coordinate across sessions work the same behind an enterprise backend as they do with a direct API key.
**What also changed in the same update:** auto mode on Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry now uses the same classifier defaults as the Anthropic API. Long foreground `sleep` commands are blocked on these platforms (same behavior as the direct API now). If you have an automation that `sleep`s between steps, replace it with a Monitor poll:
``` Monitor(command="until [ -f .done ]; do sleep 2; done") ```
**Limits:** Monitor still doesn't work in `claude mcp serve` mode. Auto mode Monitor allow-rules are set aside while auto mode is active, so Monitor commands on Bedrock go through the same classifier review as Bash commands — allow rules you set for Monitor don't bypass auto-mode review.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Monitor tool reference — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference)

item.title: Your LangGraph Agent Crashes the Whole Graph When One Node Times Out — v1.2 Adds Per-Node Timeouts and Error Handlers That Route to Recovery Nodes
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: LangGraph v1.2 ships per-node timeouts, error handlers that route to recovery nodes, and graceful shutdown that saves a resumable checkpoint — a stuck node no longer crashes the whole graph.
item.content:encoded:
**LangGraph v1.2 ships per-node timeouts, error handlers that route to recovery nodes instead of crashing the whole graph, and graceful shutdown that saves a resumable checkpoint.**
Before v1.2, an unhandled exception or stuck API call in any node crashed the entire graph unless you wrapped every node in `try/except`. The new fault-tolerance primitives handle this at the graph level.
**Per-node timeout — async nodes only:**
```python from datetime import timedelta
builder.add_node( "call_external_api", call_api_node, timeout=timedelta(seconds=30) # raises NodeTimeoutError after 30s ) ```
`NodeTimeoutError` subclasses Python's built-in `TimeoutError`, so existing retry policies catch it by default. Adding a timeout to a sync node raises an error at `compile()` time — async-only.
**Node-level error handler with routing:**
```python from langgraph.types import Command, NodeError
async def handle_api_failure(state: MyState, error: NodeError) -> Command: return Command( update={"last_error": str(error.original_error)}, goto="fallback_node" # route to a recovery node )
builder.add_node( "call_external_api", call_api_node, timeout=timedelta(seconds=30), error_handler=handle_api_failure ) ```
The handler runs only after all retries are exhausted. If the process crashes before the handler finishes, the failure context is saved in the checkpoint — on resume, the handler sees the same `NodeError`.
**Graph-wide defaults and graceful shutdown:**
```python # Set defaults for all nodes; per-node values override at compile time builder.set_node_defaults(timeout=60.0, retry=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3))
# Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM from langgraph.types import RunControl control = RunControl() signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda *_: control.request_drain()) # request_drain() waits for the current superstep, saves a resumable # checkpoint, and raises GraphDrained — no lost work ```
**Why it matters for this reader:** LangGraph graphs that call external APIs, run unattended in CI, or span overnight runs previously needed per-node defense. Now the graph itself handles failures, and a SIGTERM during a long agent run doesn't mean starting over from scratch.
**Caveats:** Timeouts are async-only; error handlers can't themselves have error handlers (prevents recursion); graceful shutdown requires wiring in `RunControl`, which is a new setup step.
**Sources:** [Fault tolerance in LangGraph — docs.langchain.com](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance) · [LangChain October 2026 newsletter — langchain.com/blog](https://www.langchain.com/blog/october-2026-langchain-newsletter) · [Community thread on parallel-node failures — forum.langchain.com](https://forum.langchain.com/t/parallel-nodes-how-to-manage-failures-or-exceptions/3226)

item.title: Your LLM App Has No Regression Tests — inspect-ai Writes an Eval in 30 Lines: Task, Solver, Scorer, Run
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: pip install inspect-ai; define a @task returning Task(dataset, solver, scorer); run inspect eval to grade any model against your inputs and catch regressions before users do.
item.content:encoded:
**pip install inspect-ai; define a @task returning Task(dataset, solver, scorer); run `inspect eval` to grade any model against your inputs and catch regressions before they reach users.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Write a repeatable LLM eval that runs against Claude, OpenAI, or a local Ollama model with one flag swap - Grade model outputs against expected answers — exact match, substring, or a second model as judge - Spot regressions when you change a system prompt, swap models, or update your context pipeline
## The 30-line eval
```python from inspect_ai import task from inspect_ai.dataset import Sample from inspect_ai.solver import generate, system_message from inspect_ai.scorer import includes, model_graded_qa from inspect_ai.task import Task
@task def qa_regression(): return Task( dataset=[ Sample( input="What is the output of list(range(3))?", target="[0, 1, 2]" ), Sample( input="Write a one-liner to reverse a Python list.", target="returns reversed list" ), ], solver=[ system_message("Answer concisely and precisely."), generate() ], scorer=includes() # target string must appear in the model output ) ```
Run it: `inspect eval qa_regression.py --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`
Swap models without touching the file: `--model openai/gpt-4o` or `--model ollama/llama3.2`.
## Scorers: choosing the right one
| Scorer | Use when | Cost | |---|---|---| | `match()` | Exact or case-insensitive string | None | | `includes()` | Target appears anywhere in output | None | | `model_graded_qa()` | No single correct string; prose or code | One model call per sample |
```python # Use a cheaper model to grade to keep costs manageable scorer=model_graded_qa( model="anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5", instructions="Grade: does the response correctly solve the task?" ) ```
## Reviewing runs
`inspect view` opens a local web UI showing per-sample grading, the full conversation, and scorer reasoning — useful for finding systematic failure patterns.
## Three limits to know
1. `model_graded_qa()` adds a model call per sample; grading cost can match eval cost at scale. Use `includes()` or `match()` where possible. 2. Pin your `inspect-ai` version — the scorer API changed between 0.3.x releases. 3. Multi-agent evals with sandboxed tool use require Docker or another sandbox provider as an extra setup step.
inspect-ai is maintained by the UK AI Security Institute and ships with 200+ pre-built eval sets (Inspect Evals), including MMLU, HumanEval, and the safety benchmarks the institute uses for its own frontier-model testing.
**Sources:** [inspect-ai Tutorial — inspect.aisi.org.uk](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/tutorial.html) · [Inspect AI: An OSS Python Library For LLM Evals — hamel.dev](https://hamel.dev/notes/llm/evals/inspect.html) (independent practitioner review with creator guest lecture video)

item.title: Your Complex Analysis Keeps Returning a Flat Wrong Answer — `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}` Shows the Full Reasoning Chain Before the Final Response
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Add thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: 10000} to your Messages API call; Claude returns thinking blocks with its full reasoning before the answer — useful for debugging incorrect analysis and auditing multi-step decisions.
item.content:encoded:
**Add `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}` to your Messages API call; Claude returns `thinking` content blocks showing its full reasoning chain before the final answer — useful for debugging incorrect analysis, auditing multi-step decisions, and understanding where a complex call went wrong.**
When Claude gives a wrong or unexpectedly shallow answer to a complex problem — code review, multi-document analysis, a logic chain — the response alone does not show where the reasoning broke down. Extended thinking surfaces the internal scratchpad so you can inspect the path, not just the conclusion.
**Enable it in Python:**
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=16000, thinking={ "type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 10000 # reasoning scratchpad budget; soft target }, messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": "Review this function for subtle bugs and edge cases: ..." }] )
for block in response.content: if block.type == "thinking": print("Reasoning:", block.thinking) # the trace — store this alongside the answer elif block.type == "text": print("Answer:", block.text) ```
**Track actual token spend:**
```python thinking_tokens = response.usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens print(f"Used {thinking_tokens} thinking tokens out of {10000} budget") ```
Thinking tokens count toward your output total. Set `budget_tokens` to match problem complexity: skip it for fast lookups, use 5,000–16,000 for long-form code review or multi-document analysis.
**When the trace pays off:**
- Debugging wrong conclusions: the trace shows the exact step where the reasoning went sideways, which is faster to fix than re-prompting blind - Multi-step reasoning where intermediate conclusions matter: store the thinking block alongside the answer for audit - Validating that Claude found the right sub-problem before it answered the main one
**Limits:** `budget_tokens` is a minimum target, not a ceiling — actual thinking token use may exceed it, raising costs proportionally. Extended thinking increases latency; a 10,000-token budget adds roughly 5–15 seconds to a typical call. The `thinking` parameter is not available on all model versions; on Claude 5.x, thinking is adaptive by default and the parameter format differs — check the [extended thinking models docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/extended-thinking-models) for version-specific details. A wrong conclusion that persists through extended thinking is a harder problem: the trace gives you the failure mode, but fixing it still requires a better prompt or a different approach.
**Sources:** [Extended thinking — docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/extended-thinking) · [Extended thinking on Amazon Bedrock — docs.aws.eu](https://docs.aws.eu/bedrock/latest/userguide/claude-messages-extended-thinking.html) (independent implementation reference)

item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic filed its public Form S-1 with the SEC on October 26, beginning the formal IPO process. For engineers building products on the Claude API, the risk factors section is the most useful part — legally required to enumerate every material uncertainty the company faces.**
After a confidential draft filed in June 2026, Anthropic published the full prospectus on October 26 ([anthropic.com/news/s1-sec](https://www.anthropic.com/news/s1-sec)), with the filing available on EDGAR.
Unlike a vendor blog post, a prospectus enumerates material risks in a legally binding document: API availability, pricing methodology, model availability under export controls (Fable 5 was suspended under US export rules in June before being reinstated in July), and the cost basis of maintaining the safety infrastructure underlying all models.
The company most recently raised at a roughly $965 billion valuation (per its Series H round), with reportedly more than $60 billion sought in the offering.

item.title: Your Cloud Inference Meter Keeps Running During Development — Ollama Runs Any Open Model Locally in One Command With a Drop-In OpenAI-Compatible Python API
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Ollama downloads and runs Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and 200+ open models locally — no API key, no per-token billing. One command installs the model; the Python library mirrors the OpenAI SDK interface exactly.
item.content:encoded:
**Ollama runs any open model — Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek, and 200+ others — on your own hardware with a single CLI command. No API key, no per-token billing during development, and a Python client whose interface mirrors the OpenAI SDK.**
## What you will be able to do after this: - Pull and run an open model in under 60 seconds with `ollama pull llama3.2` - Call it from Python with the native `ollama` library or the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at `localhost:11434/v1` - Swap between local models by changing a string — no code restructuring
## Install and pull a model
```bash # macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
# Windows: MSI installer at ollama.com/download/windows ollama pull llama3.2 # ~2 GB, Q4_K_M quantization by default ollama run llama3.2 # verify it works interactively ```
Ollama stores models in `~/.ollama/models` and serves them at `http://localhost:11434`. It selects the fastest backend automatically — Metal on Apple Silicon, CUDA on NVIDIA, CPU otherwise.
## Call it from Python — native library
```bash pip install ollama ```
```python import ollama
response = ollama.chat( model='llama3.2', messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Explain vector similarity in two sentences.'}] ) print(response.message.content) ```
`ollama.chat()` is synchronous; the async variant is `ollama.AsyncClient().chat()`. For single-turn completions without message history, use `ollama.generate()`.
## Drop-in OpenAI SDK swap
Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at `:11434/v1`. Existing code that uses the OpenAI Python SDK works with a `base_url` change:
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( base_url='http://localhost:11434/v1', api_key='ollama', # required field; value is ignored locally )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model='llama3.2', messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Explain vector similarity.'}] ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
LangChain, LlamaIndex, and other OpenAI-compatible wrappers work the same way — swap `base_url` and `model`, keep everything else.
## Browse available models
```bash ollama pull qwen2.5:7b # Alibaba Qwen 2.5 at 7B ollama pull gemma3:4b # Google Gemma 3 at 4B; fits in ~6 GB VRAM ollama pull deepseek-r1 # DeepSeek R1 distilled variants ```
Full catalog at [ollama.com/search](https://ollama.com/search). Use `:tag` for size variants: `llama3.2:1b` vs `llama3.2:3b`.
**Limits:** The first request after an idle period loads the model from disk into VRAM — 5–15 seconds for 7B+ models. Ollama runs one model per GPU by default, so concurrent requests queue. If you need high-throughput serving, multi-model GPU sharing, or concurrent users, vLLM ([covered Oct 24](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-24-04-vllm-eagle3-speculative-decoding-draft-tokens-latency)) handles that better. Ollama is purpose-built for single-developer local use, not multi-user production serving.
**Sources:** [Ollama API docs](https://docs.ollama.com/api/introduction) · [ollama-python GitHub](https://github.com/ollama/ollama-python) · [Run LLMs Locally — analyticsvidhya.com](https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/blog/2025/01/how-to-run-llm-locally/) (independent walkthrough)

item.title: Your Fine-Tuned Model's Benchmark Numbers Hide Whether It Actually Improved on YOUR Task — `evaluate.load("rouge")` Runs That Comparison in Five Lines
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Use evaluate.load("rouge") and evaluate.load("bertscore") to compare your fine-tuned checkpoint against the base model on your own held-out test set — public benchmarks won't catch regressions on your specific task.
item.content:encoded:
**Running your fine-tuned model against a public benchmark tells you whether it matches the average benchmark task — not whether it improved on yours. `evaluate.load("rouge")` and `evaluate.load("bertscore")` from HuggingFace's `evaluate` library compare your fine-tuned checkpoint against the base model on your own held-out test set in about five lines.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:**
- Run both ROUGE and BERTScore comparisons between base and fine-tuned models on a held-out split you supply - Interpret which metric signals improvement on your task versus generic text quality - Know the limits of each metric before presenting results
**Install**
```bash pip install evaluate bert_score ```
**Load metrics and run the comparison**
```python import evaluate from transformers import pipeline
rouge = evaluate.load("rouge") bertscore = evaluate.load("bertscore", lang="en")
# Load both checkpoints base_pipe = pipeline("text2text-generation", model="google/flan-t5-base") ft_pipe = pipeline("text2text-generation", model="./my-fine-tuned-checkpoint")
# Your held-out test set — never seen during fine-tuning inputs = ["Summarize: " + doc for doc in test_docs] references = test_summaries # ground-truth outputs
# Generate base_preds = [base_pipe(inp)[0]["generated_text"] for inp in inputs] ft_preds = [ft_pipe(inp)[0]["generated_text"] for inp in inputs]
# Compute base_rouge = rouge.compute(predictions=base_preds, references=references) ft_rouge = rouge.compute(predictions=ft_preds, references=references)
base_bert = bertscore.compute(predictions=base_preds, references=references) ft_bert = bertscore.compute(predictions=ft_preds, references=references)
print("ROUGE-L — base:", round(base_rouge["rougeL"], 3), " fine-tuned:", round(ft_rouge["rougeL"], 3)) print("BERTScore F1 (mean) — base:", round(sum(base_bert["f1"]) / len(base_bert["f1"]), 3), " fine-tuned:", round(sum(ft_bert["f1"]) / len(ft_bert["f1"]), 3)) print("BERTScore hashcode:", ft_bert["hashcode"]) # report for reproducibility ```
The two metrics are complementary on different failure modes. ROUGE-L measures longest-common-subsequence overlap — good at catching whether key phrases appear, blind to paraphrases and synonyms. BERTScore computes cosine similarity between contextual embeddings — catches semantic equivalence ROUGE misses, but is domain-sensitive.
**Limits**
- **ROUGE is blind to synonyms.** "automobile" and "car" score zero overlap — it penalizes paraphrases that are semantically correct. - **BERTScore is domain-dependent.** The default scoring model (`roberta-large`) was trained on general English; for biomedical or legal text, use a domain-matched model and always report the hashcode so results are reproducible. - Neither metric replaces human evaluation for the final decision — use them to surface regressions and rank candidates, not to certify readiness. - Public benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag) measure general capability; a fine-tune regression on your specific task can be invisible on benchmarks but visible here.
**Sources:** [HuggingFace `evaluate` — Transformers integrations](https://huggingface.co/docs/evaluate/transformers_integrations) · [BERTScore metric card — huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co/spaces/evaluate-metric/bertscore) · [Fine-tune evaluation patterns 2026 — ai2table.com](https://ai2table.com/fine-tune-evaluation-2026)

item.content:encoded:
**Claude Agent SDK v0.3.302 (Oct 16) flipped two defaults: forked subagents are now on by default, and fresh installs without an explicit `permissionMode` now start in default mode instead of auto.**
If you upgraded silently via `pnpm up` or a floating version range, check two things:
1. **Forked subagents on by default.** Previously opt-in, fork mode now applies automatically to spawned subagents. **Why it matters:** Silent behavior changes in SDK minor versions are the kind of regression that passes local tests but surprises you in a CI or scheduled-task environment. Both changes move the defaults toward safer unattended use, but neither is opt-out-proof for existing code.

item.title: Your Agent Forgets Every Conversation — mem0's Open-Source Memory Class Gives It Persistent Cross-Session Context in Three Lines
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: mem0's open-source Memory class stores extracted facts per user_id and retrieves them by semantic search — m.add(messages, user_id) then m.search(query, filters) before every LLM call.
item.content:encoded:
**`mem0`'s `Memory` class stores extracted facts per `user_id` and retrieves them by semantic search — `m.add(messages, user_id="alice")` then `m.search(query, filters={"user_id": "alice"})` before every LLM call gives your agent persistent context that survives process restarts.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** write agents that remember user preferences, past decisions, and ongoing project context across separate sessions without building a custom memory system.
- **mem0 extracts facts automatically.** You pass a message list and a `user_id`; mem0 calls an LLM internally (GPT-4.1-nano by default, swappable to Claude or Ollama models via config) to extract memorable facts and stores them in a local Qdrant vector database. - **Search returns ranked memories.** Before each LLM call, search for memories relevant to the current turn; results are short fact strings you inject directly into the system prompt. - **Cross-session by design.** The Qdrant store persists to disk between runs; `Memory()` with no args reconnects to the same store on every instantiation.
**Install and run**
```bash pip install mem0ai ```
```python from mem0 import Memory
m = Memory()
# After the agent replies, store the exchange m.add( messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Use PostgreSQL for this project, not MySQL."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Noted. I'll use PostgreSQL throughout."}, ], user_id="alice", )
# Before the next LLM call, retrieve relevant memories results = m.search("database choice", filters={"user_id": "alice"}) context = "\n".join(r["memory"] for r in results["results"]) # context: "User prefers PostgreSQL over MySQL." ```
Prepend `context` to the system prompt: `"What you know about this user:\n" + context`.
**Limits**
- Default backends: OpenAI `gpt-4.1-nano` (extraction), `text-embedding-3-small` (vectors), Qdrant (storage), SQLite (history). All swappable — the [configuration docs](https://docs.mem0.ai/open-source/overview) cover Anthropic, Ollama, and pgvector backends. - The open-source version has no rate limits on local runs, but graph memory (entity-relationship graphs across sessions) requires the hosted tier. - Each `add()` call costs one extra LLM call for fact extraction. On short exchanges the overhead is negligible; on long conversations watch latency and cost. - Memory quality depends on the extraction LLM. A cheap default may miss nuanced facts; swap to a more capable model for production use cases where precision matters.
**Sources:** [mem0 open-source Python quickstart — docs.mem0.ai](https://docs.mem0.ai/open-source/python-quickstart) · [Build Long-Term Memory in AI Agents with LangGraph and Mem0 — DigitalOcean / DEV Community](https://dev.to/digitalocean/tutorial-build-long-term-memory-in-ai-agents-with-langgraph-and-mem0-2ln1) · [Mem0 tutorial — datacamp.com](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/mem0-tutorial)

item.title: Your Claude Classification Call Returns Text When You Need a Schema — `tool_choice: {type: "tool"}` Eliminates the Maybe
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Set tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "fn"} with a single tool definition and Claude always calls that tool — eliminating the text-vs-tool-call branch from every classification and structured extraction pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
**Define one tool, set `tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "fn"}`, and Claude always returns that tool's schema — no text-response fallback, no parsing branch.**
When you add tools to a Claude call with `tool_choice="auto"` (the default), Claude decides whether to call a tool or answer in plain text. That's fine for open-ended agents, but it is the wrong default for classification and structured extraction: your pipeline now has to handle two response shapes, and the plain-text path breaks downstream parsing silently.
**The four `tool_choice` modes:**
```python # auto (default) — Claude decides tool_choice = "auto"
# any — Claude must call some tool tool_choice = "any"
# tool — Claude must call THIS specific tool tool_choice = {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_issue"}
# none — Claude must not call any tool (text only) tool_choice = "none" ```
**Practical example — support ticket classifier:**
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
tools = [{ "name": "classify_issue", "description": "Classify a support ticket", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "category": { "type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "technical", "feature_request", "other"] }, "urgency": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high"]}, "summary": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 120} }, "required": ["category", "urgency", "summary"] } }]
response = client.messages.create( model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=256, tools=tools, tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "classify_issue"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Login fails with 500 error after the last deploy."}] )
# Always a tool call — no text-response branch result = response.content[0].input print(result["category"], result["urgency"], result["summary"]) # → technical high Login fails with 500 after last deploy ```
Use `claude-haiku-5-5` for bulk classification — at 1M context and low cost it handles thousands of tickets per hour. Reserve Sonnet for extractions where the reasoning matters.
**Three limits to know:**
1. `tool_choice: {type: "tool"}` and `tool_choice: "any"` are incompatible with extended thinking (`betas=["thinking"]`). You can't force a tool call and get a reasoning trace in the same request. 2. Changing `tool_choice` mid-conversation invalidates the system-prompt cache block. If you have a large system prompt and want caching, pin the same `tool_choice` mode across all turns. 3. `type: "tool"` still requires the named tool to be in the `tools` array — the request errors if the name doesn't match.
**Vs. `client.messages.parse()`:** The Python SDK's `.parse()` method is cleaner if you already control the full call and use Python throughout. `tool_choice` is the right lever when you're building a low-level pipeline, calling from multiple languages, or want to keep the tool schema separately defined.
**Sources:** [Tool use — Anthropic API docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use) · [tool_choice reference — promptlayer.com](https://www.promptlayer.com/glossary/anthropic-tool-choice) · [Claude API best practices 2026 — tkmxai.it.com](https://www.tkmxai.it.com/claude-api-best-practices-checklist-for-production-ai-applications-in-2026)

item.title: Your Embedding Function Calls a Remote API on Every Lookup — sentence-transformers Runs all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Locally in Three Lines
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: sentence-transformers 5.x loads a model from HuggingFace, runs inference locally, and returns 384-dim vectors you can compare with util.semantic_search — no API key, no per-call cost, no rate limit.
item.content:encoded:
**`sentence-transformers` loads `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` locally, embeds your corpus once, and searches it with `util.semantic_search` — no API key, no per-call cost.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:**
- Produce embeddings from any text, entirely offline, with a 40 MB model that fits on a laptop - Understand what the 384-dimensional vector actually is: a fixed position in semantic space where similar sentences land near each other - Run `util.semantic_search` to get ranked hits with cosine scores, ready to pass into a vector store
---
**Install:**
```bash pip install sentence-transformers ```
**Encode a corpus and search it:**
```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
corpus = [ "How to configure a Postgres connection pool", "Deploying a Python service to Kubernetes", "Setting environment variables in Docker", "Optimizing slow database queries with EXPLAIN", ]
# Encode the corpus once — cache or store these vectors corpus_embeddings = model.encode(corpus, convert_to_tensor=True)
# Encode the query and search query = "How do I pass config to my container?" query_embedding = model.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True)
hits = util.semantic_search(query_embedding, corpus_embeddings, top_k=2) for hit in hits[0]: print(f"Score: {hit['score']:.3f} | {corpus[hit['corpus_id']]}") ```
Output: ``` Score: 0.512 | Setting environment variables in Docker Score: 0.431 | Deploying a Python service to Kubernetes ```
The query never mentioned Docker — similarity is semantic, not keyword. The model maps both "pass config to my container" and "setting environment variables in Docker" to nearby points in the same 384-dimensional space.
**How it works:** `model.encode()` runs a transformer (a small BERT variant) over each sentence and pools the token embeddings into one fixed-size vector. The model was trained to put sentences with similar meaning close together in cosine distance. That training is what makes the lookup work without any fine-tuning on your data.
**For asymmetric search (short query, long documents):** the standard `encode()` uses a symmetric model. Switch to `multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1` and call `model.encode_query()` / `model.encode_document()` — those apply the model's built-in query and document prompts, which improve retrieval when the two sides look very different in length and style.
**The next step in production:** you wouldn't recompute `corpus_embeddings` on every request. Compute once, save with `numpy.save()` or push the vectors into Qdrant/pgvector, then call your vector store's ANN index instead of `util.semantic_search`. The `util.semantic_search` call above is a brute-force cosine scan — fine for a few hundred documents, slow beyond that.
**Limits:**
- `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` has a 256-token max sequence length. Documents longer than that need chunking before embedding — use `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` (covered earlier) and embed each chunk separately. - CPU inference is workable for small corpora but slow at scale. If you're embedding millions of chunks, use a GPU or a hosted embedding API; sentence-transformers ships CUDA support if a GPU is available. - The model is not multilingual. For non-English text use `paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2` (same size, 50+ languages).
**Sources:** [sentence-transformers quickstart — sbert.net](https://sbert.net/docs/quickstart.html) · [Semantic search examples — sbert.net](https://www.sbert.net/examples/applications/semantic-search/README.html) · [all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card — HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2)

item.title: REVIEW.md Is How You Tell Claude Code Review What Actually Matters in Your Codebase
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: The GitHub App reads both CLAUDE.md and REVIEW.md. The local /code-review command reads only CLAUDE.md. Knowing that split is how you make PR reviews useful without adding noise to local analysis.
item.content:encoded:
**The Claude Code Review GitHub App reads two files when it reviews a PR: `CLAUDE.md` and `REVIEW.md`. The local `/code-review` command reads only `CLAUDE.md`. Knowing this split is how you make PR reviews useful without adding noise to local analysis.**
`REVIEW.md` is the PR-review-only configuration layer. It sits in your repo root on the default branch and tells the GitHub App what counts as important — without affecting how Claude Code analyzes diffs locally.
**A working REVIEW.md:**
```markdown # Review instructions
## What Important means here Reserve Important for findings that would break behavior, leak data, or block a rollback: incorrect logic, unscoped database queries, PII in logs or error messages, and migrations that aren't backward compatible. Style, naming, and refactoring suggestions are Nit at most.
## Cap the nits Report at most five Nits per review.
## Do not report - Anything CI already enforces: lint, formatting, type errors - Generated files under src/gen/ and any *.lock file - Test-only code that intentionally violates production rules
## Always check - New API routes have an integration test - Log lines don't include email addresses, user IDs, or request bodies - Database queries are scoped to the caller's tenant ```
**Three things REVIEW.md can do that CLAUDE.md cannot:**
1. **Cap the nit count.** "Report at most five Nits per review" applies only to the GitHub App — the local `/code-review` command has no such cap. 2. **Exclude generated files.** Protect `*.lock`, `src/gen/`, or migration files from noise-generating findings. 3. **Add subdirectory rules.** A `backend/REVIEW.md` adds checks specifically for changes under `backend/` — additive to the root file, not a replacement.
**Two things to know before shipping REVIEW.md:**
- **The file is read from the base/default branch, not from the PR.** A `REVIEW.md` added in a PR itself does not take effect — it must already exist on `main` (or your default branch). - **Nit caps and path exclusions require a protected branch.** Without branch protection, the App ignores those directives. Check your branch settings first.
You can also pull in skill files: `@.claude/skills/steward/SKILL.md` loads a per-repo review checklist that both the GitHub App and the babysit/steward system share.
**Sources:** [Customize Claude Code Review — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-customize)

item.title: Your Claude Agent SDK Has Zero Observability by Default — Three Lines Add Full Traces to Phoenix
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Every query() call your Claude Agent SDK makes runs in a black box unless you instrument it. Phoenix — Arize's open-source LLM observability platform — adds full span traces in three setup lines.
item.content:encoded:
**Every `query()` call your Claude Agent SDK makes runs in a black box unless you instrument it. Phoenix — Arize's open-source LLM observability platform — adds full span traces in three setup lines.**
Install the OpenInference instrumentation package alongside your SDK:
```bash pip install openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk claude-agent-sdk arize-phoenix-otel ```
Then, **before any `query()` call**, register Phoenix and let it auto-instrument:
```python from phoenix.otel import register
tracer_provider = register( project_name="my-agent", auto_instrument=True, ) ```
That's it. Every subsequent `query()` call records a span: the model called, tool calls made, token counts, latency, and the full input/output. Open `http://localhost:6006` to browse traces in the Phoenix UI.
**When you need privacy controls** — to hide user inputs or agent outputs from the trace store — skip `auto_instrument` and configure the instrumentor directly:
```python from phoenix.otel import register from openinference.instrumentation.claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentSDKInstrumentor
tracer_provider = register(project_name="my-agent") ClaudeAgentSDKInstrumentor().instrument( tracer_provider=tracer_provider, hide_inputs=True, hide_outputs=True, ) ```
`hide_inputs=True` redacts the messages you send; `hide_outputs=True` redacts model responses. Spans still record timing, tool names, and token counts.
**Three things traces reveal that logs miss:**
1. **Tool call waterfalls** — which tools the agent invoked, in what order, and which ones took the most wall time. 2. **Token spend per task** — how many tokens each `query()` consumed, so you can find expensive paths before they hit your budget. 3. **Failure attribution** — when an agent task fails, the span tree shows whether the problem was in a tool call, a model refusal, or the application layer.
**Limit:** Phoenix stores traces locally by default. For a shared team view or persistence beyond a single dev session, set `PHOENIX_COLLECTOR_ENDPOINT` to point at a hosted Phoenix instance or another OTLP-compatible backend.
**Sources:** [Phoenix × Claude Agent SDK — Arize docs](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/claude-agent-sdk) · [Claude Agent SDK tracing — Phoenix docs](https://phoenix.arize.com/docs/ax/integrations/python-agent-frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/claude-agent-sdk-tracing.md) · [OpenInference instrumentation — GitHub](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference)

item.title: Anthropic's Agents Made 30,000 Commits a Day — Three Patterns That Keep Agent-Driven CI/CD From Imploding
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Anthropic's engineering post on Scion reveals what happens when agents drive commit volume beyond what git handles. Four patterns that hold up: merge queues, branch-per-task, atomic commits, fast CI.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic published the design rationale behind Scion, its in-house VCS that replaced git after agent-generated commits outpaced what git's offline-first architecture could handle. The patterns behind it apply to any agent-driven repo today.**
Git assumes clients work mostly offline with a full copy of the repository. That assumption breaks when most commits come from always-networked agents — CI jobs, coding agents, automated test runners. Secondary coverage of [Anthropic's engineering post](https://anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) reports daily merges rising to over 30,000; the post's first design principle for Scion was "clients are always online." Scion itself is internal and not open source — but the workflow patterns it was built to survive are ones you can adopt now.
**Four patterns that hold up at agent commit volume:**
**1. Turn on the merge queue.** GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket all support merge queues. Enable one on any branch where agents push concurrently. Merge queues serialize merges, eliminating the "twenty PRs, all stale from the same branch point" problem that appears the moment parallel agents each open a PR.
**2. One branch per agent task.** Claude Code does this by default via git worktrees. If you're building your own pipeline, give each agent task a fresh branch at task start. Shared feature branches accumulate mid-task conflicts when two tasks run in parallel.
**3. Atomic commits.** Agents shouldn't accumulate 50-file diffs any more than humans should. Keep each commit to one purpose: a CI task that breaks can be reverted cleanly, and a code review tool can reason about a targeted change.
**4. Make CI fast.** At human commit rates, a 10-minute CI run is annoying. At agent commit rates, it becomes a merge-queue bottleneck that backs up indefinitely. Profile the slowest check in your critical path and target under 2 minutes.
**Limit:** These patterns reduce friction; they don't replace a solid test suite. A fast, broken CI is worse than a slow, accurate one.
